[Appendix D: Further Reading](#appendix-d-further-reading)\n\n---\n\n## Part 1: The Big Picture — Database Parity in a Multi-Tenant AI Platform\n\n### Chapter 1: Why Three Database Engines?\n\nbchat began as a single-tenant, single-binary application built on SQLite. The original `memos` project used SQLite exclusively — it was simple, embedded, zero-ops. As the project evolved into a multi-tenant AI chat platform, two things happened:\n\n1. **PostgreSQL was added** for production deployments. The decision to use Postgres over MySQL was driven by Fly.io's native Postgres support, connection pooling via PgBouncer, and the need for concurrent write throughput that SQLite could not provide in a multi-process deployment.\n\n2. **MySQL was added** as a third option. The `go-sql-driver/mysql` dependency was added to `go.mod`, a MySQL `LATEST.sql` was created with the core Memos schema, and stub implementations were written for all agent features. But MySQL parity for the agent system was never completed.\n\n**Your goal in this tutorial** is to understand what \"database parity\" means in a Go application that uses the `database/sql` standard library, and to port the missing parity to MySQL yourself. Along the way you will confront questions about migration strategy, SQL dialect portability, testing, and production operations.\n\n#### The Three-Tier Pattern\n\nEvery database-backed Go application with multiple backend support follows this pattern:\n\n```\n┌─────────────────────┐\n│   store.Driver      │  ← Interface (the contract)\n├─────────────────────┤\n│ SQLite  │ Postgres  │  MySQL     ← Implementations\n├─────────────────────┤\n│ sqlite/ │ postgres/ │ mysql/     ← Packages\n└─────────────────────┘\n```\n\nbchat follows this pattern with an important twist: instead of three full implementations, it has **2.3 implementations**. SQLite and Postgres are complete. MySQL has full coverage of the core Memos tables (user, memo, resource, etc.) but all agent-specific features are stubs.\n\nThis is not necessarily a bad thing. Not all backends need all features. The question is: **when is parity important, and when is it premature?**\n\n#### Questions to Ask Before Porting\n\nBefore we look at a single line of code, ask yourself:\n\n- Who is asking for MySQL support? A specific customer on PlanetScale? An internal requirement for MySQL compatibility? Or just \"completeness\"?\n- What features do they actually need? All agent features? Just the chat endpoint? Just the webhook integration?\n- What is the cost of not porting? Error messages returned to users? Silent data loss? No deployment at all?\n- What is the maintenance burden of adding a third backend to every future feature? Every new store method must be implemented three times.\n\nKeep these questions in your pocket. We will revisit them in Chapter 18.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 2: The Driver Interface Contract\n\nThe entire database parity system rests on a single Go interface in `store/driver.go`:\n\n```go\ntype Driver interface {\n    GetDB() *sql.DB\n    Close() error\n\n    // Core Memos models\n    FindMigrationHistoryList(ctx context.Context, find *FindMigrationHistory) ([]*MigrationHistory, error)\n    UpsertMigrationHistory(ctx context.Context, upsert *UpsertMigrationHistory) (*MigrationHistory, error)\n    CreateActivity(ctx context.Context, create *Activity) (*Activity, error)\n    ListActivities(ctx context.Context, find *FindActivity) ([]*Activity, error)\n    CreateResource(ctx context.Context, create *Resource) (*Resource, error)\n    ListResources(ctx context.Context, find *FindResource) ([]*Resource, error)\n    CreateMemo(ctx context.Context, create *Memo) (*Memo, error)\n    ListMemos(ctx context.Context, find *FindMemo) ([]*Memo, error)\n    // ... ~180 methods total\n}\n```\n\nThis is a **fat interface** — it contains every database operation across every domain in the application. The tradeoff is clear:\n\n- **Pro:** One contract. Any backend that satisfies it can be swapped in via the factory. No dependency injection framework needed.\n- **Con:** Every new feature adds methods to the interface, which means every backend must be updated. A backend that doesn't support a feature still needs a stub.\n\n#### The Factory Pattern\n\nThe factory lives in `store/db/db.go`:\n\n```go\nfunc NewDBDriver(profile *profile.Profile) (store.Driver, error) {\n    var driver store.Driver\n    var err error\n\n    switch profile.Driver {\n    case \"sqlite\":\n        driver, err = sqlite.NewDB(profile)\n    case \"mysql\":\n        driver, err = mysql.NewDB(profile)\n    case \"postgres\":\n        driver, err = postgres.NewDB(profile)\n    default:\n        return nil, errors.New(\"unknown db driver\")\n    }\n    if err != nil {\n        return nil, errors.Wrap(err, \"failed to create db driver\")\n    }\n    return driver, nil\n}\n```\n\nThe `profile.Driver` value comes from the application's configuration (`internal/profile/profile.go`):\n\n```go\ntype Profile struct {\n    Mode    string // \"prod\", \"dev\", \"demo\"\n    Driver  string // \"sqlite\", \"mysql\", \"postgres\"\n    DSN     string // Data Source Name\n    // ...\n}\n\nfunc (p *Profile) Validate() error {\n    if p.Driver == \"sqlite\" && p.DSN == \"\" {\n        dbFile := fmt.Sprintf(\"memos_%s.db\", p.Mode)\n        p.DSN = filepath.Join(dataDir, dbFile)\n    }\n    if p.Driver == \"postgres\" && p.DSN == \"\" {\n        p.DSN = os.Getenv(\"DATABASE_URL\")\n        if p.DSN == \"\" {\n            return errors.New(\"postgres driver requires DSN or DATABASE_URL\")\n        }\n    }\n    // Note: MySQL has no fallback — the user must provide DSN explicitly\n    return nil\n}\n```\n\nNotice that MySQL has no DSN fallback. This is a small signal: MySQL support was added but never made it into the default startup flow.\n\n#### Connection Setup Differences\n\nEach backend creates its own `*sql.DB` with different drivers:\n\n| Backend | Driver | Import | Connection Setup |\n|---------|--------|--------|-----------------|\n| SQLite | `github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3` | CGO required | File path as DSN, `_journal_mode=WAL` |\n| Postgres | `github.com/jackc/pgx/v5` | Pure Go | Connection string from `DATABASE_URL` |\n| MySQL | `github.com/go-sql-driver/mysql` | Pure Go | DSN parsed, `multiStatements=true` for migrations |\n\nThe MySQL connection setup in `store/db/mysql/mysql.go`:\n\n```go\nfunc NewDB(profile *profile.Profile) (store.Driver, error) {\n    dsn, err := mergeDSN(profile.DSN)\n    if err != nil {\n        return nil, err\n    }\n    // ...\n    driver.db, err = sql.Open(\"mysql\", dsn)\n    // ...\n}\n\nfunc mergeDSN(baseDSN string) (string, error) {\n    config, err := mysql.ParseDSN(baseDSN)\n    if err != nil {\n        return \"\", errors.Wrapf(err, \"failed to parse DSN: %s\", baseDSN)\n    }\n    config.MultiStatements = true  // Required for migration files with multiple SQL statements\n    return config.FormatDSN(), nil\n}\n```\n\nKey observation: the MySQL connection forces `MultiStatements = true` because the migration system executes multiple SQL statements per file. This is a security concern — it means SQL injection via the migration system is possible if user input ever enters migration files (it shouldn't, but the surface area is larger).\n\n---\n\n## Part 2: Anatomy of the Parity Gap\n\n### Chapter 3: The Schema Gap\n\nThe easiest way to see the parity gap is to compare the `LATEST.sql` files across all three backends:\n\n| Metric | SQLite | Postgres | MySQL |\n|--------|--------|----------|-------|\n| Lines of SQL | 1,067 | 960 | 132 |\n| Agent tables | 30+ | 30+ | **0** |\n| RBAC tables | Yes | Yes | No |\n| Bridge tables | Yes | Yes | No |\n| Migration directories | 32 versions | 14 versions | 11 versions |\n| Latest migration | 0.31 | 0.31 | 0.25 |\n\nThe MySQL `LATEST.sql` at `store/migration/mysql/LATEST.sql` contains only the original Memos tables:\n\n```sql\n-- migration_history\nCREATE TABLE `migration_history` (\n  `version` VARCHAR(256) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,\n  `created_ts` TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP\n);\n\n-- user\nCREATE TABLE `user` (\n  `id` INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,\n  `username` VARCHAR(256) NOT NULL UNIQUE,\n  `role` VARCHAR(256) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USER',\n  `password_hash` VARCHAR(256) NOT NULL,\n  ...\n);\n\n-- memo\nCREATE TABLE `memo` (\n  `id` INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,\n  `uid` VARCHAR(256) NOT NULL UNIQUE,\n  `creator_id` INT NOT NULL,\n  `content` TEXT NOT NULL,\n  `visibility` VARCHAR(256) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PRIVATE',\n  `payload` JSON NOT NULL,\n  ...\n);\n\n-- resource, activity, idp, inbox, webhook, reaction...\n```\n\nThat's it. No `agent_tenants`, no `agent_audiences`, no `agent_sessions`, no `agent_integrations`, no `agent_events`, no bridge tables, no RBAC, no observational memory, no workflows, no QA pairs, no transcripts, no leads, no reindex checkpoints.\n\nCompare with the SQLite schema at `store/migration/sqlite/LATEST.sql` which spans agent tables at lines 201–1067. The agent tables alone include:\n\n- `agent_tenants` — tenant definitions\n- `agent_audiences` — per-tenant audience configuration\n- `agent_services` — service catalog entries\n- `agent_exclusions` — service exclusions\n- `agent_coverage` — geographic coverage\n- `agent_faqs` — FAQ entries\n- `agent_safety_protocols` — safety instructions\n- `agent_kb_sections` — knowledge base sections\n- `agent_intents` — customer intents\n- `agent_rules` — behavioral rules\n- `agent_sessions` — chat sessions\n- `agent_source_files` — KB/Policy/Script versioned files\n- `agent_rate_limits` — per-IP rate limiting\n- `agent_simulations` — simulation runs\n- `agent_tenant_scripts` — conversation scripts\n- `agent_script_analysis` — script compliance analysis\n- `agent_qa_pairs` — Q&A pairs for embedding testing\n- `agent_transcripts` — chat conversation transcripts\n- `agent_leads` — captured leads\n- `agent_workflows` — ticket workflows\n- `agent_simulation_transcripts` — simulation transcripts\n- `agent_analysis_results` — conversation analysis\n- `agent_learning_memory` — learned patterns\n- `agent_compliance_audits` — compliance audit results\n- `agent_scoring_config` — scoring configuration\n- `agent_reindex_checkpoints` — RAG reindex resume points\n- `agent_observations` — observational memory\n- `bridge_external_sessions` — external bridge sessions\n- `bridge_handoffs` — handoff management\n- `bridge_auth_keys` — bridge HMAC authentication\n- `bridge_auth_nonces` — replay protection\n- `bridge_handoff_replies` — handoff replies\n- `bridge_reply_outbox` — outbox pattern for delivery\n- `agent_messages` — deduplicated message store\n- `agent_integrations` — webhook integrations (migration 31)\n- `agent_events` — webhook events (migration 31)\n\n#### Migration Version Gap\n\nThe MySQL migration directory at `store/migration/mysql/` stops at version `0.25`:\n\n```\nstore/migration/mysql/          store/migration/sqlite/\n├── 0.17/                        ├── 0.17/\n├── 0.18/                        ├── 0.18/\n├── 0.19/                        ├── 0.19/\n├── 0.20/                        ├── 0.20/\n├── 0.21/                        ├── 0.21/\n├── 0.22/                        ├── 0.22/\n├── 0.23/                        ├── 0.23/\n├── 0.24/                        ├── 0.24/\n├── 0.25/                        ├── 0.25/\n└── LATEST.sql                   ├── 0.26/\n                                 ├── 0.27/\n                                 ├── 0.28/\n                                 ├── 0.29/\n                                 ├── 0.30/\n                                 └── 0.31/\n```\n\nEvery version from 0.26 to 0.31 added agent-specific tables, RBAC, bridge delivery, integrations, and events. The MySQL backend never received corresponding migrations.\n\n**Key insight:** The migration system per-driver paths (e.g., `migration/postgres/`, `migration/sqlite/`) mean that adding MySQL migrations does not cause merge conflicts with other backends. Each backend's migration files are independent. The tradeoff is that you must maintain `n` copies of each migration.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 4: The Implementation Gap\n\nThe schema gap is visible from the file tree. The implementation gap requires reading the code.\n\n#### Agent Methods: All Stubbed\n\nThe MySQL agent implementation at `store/db/mysql/agent.go` is 449 lines of this pattern:\n\n```go\nvar errNotImplemented = errors.New(\"agent features not implemented for MySQL\")\n\nfunc (d *DB) CreateAgentTenant(ctx context.Context, tenant *store.AgentTenant) (*store.AgentTenant, error) {\n    return nil, errNotImplemented\n}\n\nfunc (d *DB) GetAgentTenant(ctx context.Context, find *store.FindAgentTenant) (*store.AgentTenant, error) {\n    return nil, errNotImplemented\n}\n\nfunc (d *DB) ListAgentTenants(ctx context.Context, find *store.FindAgentTenant) ([]*store.AgentTenant, error) {\n    return nil, errNotImplemented\n}\n\nfunc (d *DB) UpdateAgentTenant(ctx context.Context, tenant *store.AgentTenant) (*store.AgentTenant, error) {\n    return nil, errNotImplemented\n}\n\nfunc (d *DB) DeleteAgentTenant(ctx context.Context, id int32) error {\n    return errNotImplemented\n}\n```\n\nEvery single agent method follows this pattern. There are approximately 70 such methods covering tenants, audiences, services, exclusions, coverage, FAQs, safety protocols, KB sections, intents, rules, sessions, source files, simulations, transcripts, analysis, learning memory, compliance audits, scoring config, QA pairs, leads, reindex checkpoints, integrations, and events.\n\n#### Rate Limiting: Fail-Open\n\nTwo methods deviate from the `errNotImplemented` pattern — they **fail open** instead:\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) CheckAndIncrementAgentRateLimit(ctx context.Context, tenantID int32, audienceType, clientIP string, rpm int) (bool, error) {\n    slog.Warn(\"agent rate limit check not implemented for MySQL, allowing request\",\n        \"tenantID\", tenantID, \"clientIP\", clientIP, \"audienceType\", audienceType)\n    return true, nil\n}\n\nfunc (d *DB) CheckAndIncrementTenantGlobalRateLimit(ctx context.Context, tenantID int32, audienceType string, rpm int) (bool, error) {\n    slog.Warn(\"tenant global rate limit check not implemented for MySQL, allowing request\",\n        \"tenantID\", tenantID, \"audienceType\", audienceType)\n    return true, nil\n}\n```\n\nThis is a deliberate design choice: if rate limiting is not implemented, the system should allow requests rather than deny them. The warning log is there so operators notice. But in a production deployment, this is a **security gap** — any client can bypass rate limits.\n\n**Question for you:** Is fail-open the right default? What are the alternatives?\n- Fail-closed (deny all requests) — safe but breaks the feature entirely\n- Fail-open with a low static limit (max 5 RPM) — better than unlimited\n- Environment-level gate (only fail-open in dev mode, fail-closed in prod)\n\n#### Bridge Delivery: Unsupported\n\nThe MySQL bridge implementation at `store/db/mysql/bridge.go` returns `store.ErrBridgeUnsupportedDatabase` for every method:\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) EnsureBridgeExternalSession(context.Context, int32, string, time.Time, time.Time) (*store.BridgeExternalSession, bool, error) {\n    return nil, false, store.ErrBridgeUnsupportedDatabase\n}\n```\n\nThe `SupportsBridgeDelivery()` method on the MySQL driver returns `false`, which the service layer checks before attempting bridge operations.\n\n#### Agent Workflows: Silent Stubs\n\nThe MySQL agent workflow stubs at `store/db/mysql/agent_workflow.go` are the most dangerous pattern:\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) CreateAgentWorkflow(ctx context.Context, create *store.CreateAgentWorkflow) (*store.AgentWorkflow, error) {\n    return nil, nil  // TODO: Implement\n}\n\nfunc (d *DB) ListAgentWorkflows(ctx context.Context, find *store.FindAgentWorkflow) ([]*store.AgentWorkflow, error) {\n    return nil, nil  // TODO: Implement\n}\n\nfunc (d *DB) GetAgentWorkflow(ctx context.Context, find *store.FindAgentWorkflow) (*store.AgentWorkflow, error) {\n    return nil, nil  // TODO: Implement\n}\n```\n\nReturning `nil, nil` means the caller thinks the operation succeeded (no error), but gets back a nil result. Depending on the caller, this could cause nil pointer dereferences, silent data loss, or confusing \"not found\" behavior. This is worse than `errNotImplemented` because errors are visible to the operator; silent nil returns are invisible until something breaks.\n\n#### Observational Memory: Explicit Errors\n\nThe MySQL observations stubs at `store/db/mysql/agent_observations.go` return errors, but inconsistently:\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) UpsertObservationLog(ctx context.Context, log *store.ObservationLog) (*store.ObservationLog, error) {\n    return nil, fmt.Errorf(\"UpsertObservationLog not implemented for MySQL\")\n}\n```\n\nNote the use of `fmt.Errorf` instead of the `errNotImplemented` sentinel error used in agent.go. Inconsistency in error wrapping is a code review smell — it makes it harder for callers to check error types.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 5: SQL Dialect Differences at a Glance\n\nBefore we can write MySQL migrations, we need to understand the SQL dialects of all three backends. Here is the practical reference:\n\n#### Placeholders\n\n| Backend | Placeholder | Example |\n|---------|-------------|---------|\n| SQLite | `?` (positional) | `WHERE id = ?` |\n| Postgres | `$N` (numbered) | `WHERE id = $1` |\n| MySQL | `?` (positional) | `WHERE id = ?` |\n\n**MySQL is compatible with SQLite** for placeholder syntax. This means porting from SQLite to MySQL is easier than porting from Postgres to MySQL — you can reuse the SQLite query structure and only change data types and functions.\n\nPostgres uses `$1`, `$2`, ... which requires `fmt.Sprintf(\" AND id = $%d\", argIdx)` in the Go code. Both SQLite and MySQL use simple `?` and append args to a slice.\n\n#### Auto-Increment / Serial\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite\nid INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT\n\n-- Postgres\nid SERIAL PRIMARY KEY\n\n-- MySQL\nid INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY\n```\n\nMySQL can also use `BIGINT` instead of `INT` if you expect more than 2 billion rows:\n\n```sql\nid BIGINT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY\n```\n\n#### Timestamps\n\nThis is the trickiest difference. The choice is between **epoch integers** (SQLite/Postgres) and **native TIMESTAMP** (MySQL):\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite (epoch integer, stored as INTEGER)\ncreated_ts BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%s', 'now'))\n\n-- Postgres (epoch integer, stored as BIGINT)\ncreated_ts BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM NOW())\n\n-- MySQL option 1: native TIMESTAMP (stored as DATETIME)\ncreated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP\n\n-- MySQL option 2: epoch integer (to match SQLite pattern)\ncreated_ts BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT (UNIX_TIMESTAMP())\n```\n\n**bchat's SQLite schema** uses a mix of both approaches:\n- Core tables (memo, user, activity) use `BIGINT` epoch timestamps via `strftime('%s', 'now')`\n- Agent tables use `TIMESTAMP` via `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`\n- Newer agent tables (integrations, events) use `BIGINT` epoch timestamps\n\nThis inconsistency within SQLite itself is worth noting. The Postgres schema mirrors SQLite's approach, while the MySQL schema (for core tables) uses `TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`.\n\n**Your decision:** When porting agent tables to MySQL, you can choose:\n- **Match MySQL style:** Use `TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` — idiomatic MySQL, works with MySQL tools\n- **Match SQLite agent style:** Use `BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT (UNIX_TIMESTAMP())` — keeps the API consistent across backends\n\nThere is no universally correct answer. The tradeoff is between backend idiomaticity and cross-backend consistency. Both approaches are viable.\n\n#### JSON\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite\npayload TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'\n\n-- Postgres\npayload JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'\n\n-- MySQL\npayload JSON NOT NULL\n```\n\nMySQL's `JSON` type is similar to Postgres's `JSONB` — it validates JSON on insert and stores it in a binary format that allows indexing via generated columns. SQLite's `TEXT` approach works but requires application-level validation.\n\n#### Booleans\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite (0 or 1, stored as INTEGER)\nis_active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1\nCHECK (is_active IN (0, 1))\n\n-- Postgres (true/false, stored as BOOLEAN)\nis_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE\n\n-- MySQL (true/false, stored as TINYINT)\nis_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE\n-- or\nis_active TINYINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1\n```\n\nMySQL treats `BOOLEAN` as `TINYINT(1)`. Values are 0 (false) and non-zero (true). This is compatible with SQLite's integer approach — both return integers from queries.\n\n#### RETURNING Clause vs LastInsertId\n\n```go\n// SQLite: INSERT + LastInsertId\nresult, err := d.db.ExecContext(ctx, stmt, args...)\nid, err := result.LastInsertId()\n\n// Postgres: INSERT ... RETURNING id\nerr := d.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, stmt, args...).Scan(&id)\n\n// MySQL: same as SQLite pattern\nresult, err := d.db.ExecContext(ctx, stmt, args...)\nid, err := result.LastInsertId()\n```\n\nMySQL 8.0.30+ supports `RETURNING` clauses (via `VALUES ... RETURNING ...` syntax in MySQL 8.0.34+), but the existing codebase uses `LastInsertId` for SQLite, and MySQL's `database/sql` driver supports it natively. Stick with `LastInsertId` for MySQL compatibility.\n\n#### CHECK Constraints\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite: enforced\nstatus TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active', 'closed'))\n\n-- Postgres: enforced\nstatus TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active', 'closed'))\n\n-- MySQL before 8.0.16: parsed but ignored\n-- MySQL 8.0.16+: enforced\nstatus TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active', 'closed'))\n```\n\n**Critical:** If your target MySQL version is < 8.0.16, CHECK constraints are **syntactically valid but not enforced**. You must enforce constraints at the application level. PlanetScale uses Vitess, which also ignores CHECK constraints.\n\nAs of 2026, MySQL 8.0 has reached end of life and 9.0 is the current GA release. Most modern MySQL deployments (8.0.16+, 8.4+, 9.0+) enforce CHECK constraints. But if you target PlanetScale, assume they are not enforced.\n\n#### UPSERT / ON CONFLICT\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite\nINSERT INTO agent_rate_limits (...) VALUES (...)\nON CONFLICT(tenant_id, audience_type, client_ip) DO UPDATE SET request_count = request_count + 1;\n\n-- Postgres\nINSERT INTO agent_rate_limits (...) VALUES (...)\nON CONFLICT(tenant_id, audience_type, client_ip) DO UPDATE SET request_count = request_count + 1;\n\n-- MySQL\nINSERT INTO agent_rate_limits (...) VALUES (...)\nON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE request_count = request_count + 1;\n```\n\nMySQL uses `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` instead of `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`. The behavior is similar but the syntax is different.\n\n#### Identifiers\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite: unquoted or double-quoted\nSELECT * FROM user WHERE username = 'alice';\n\n-- Postgres: double-quoted (lowercase unquoted is folded to lowercase)\nSELECT * FROM \"user\" WHERE username = 'alice';\n\n-- MySQL: backtick-quoted (configurable, but backtick is standard)\nSELECT * FROM `user` WHERE username = 'alice';\n```\n\nThe MySQL backtick requirement is specific to MySQL and MariaDB. The existing MySQL implementations in the codebase use backtick-quoted identifiers, which is the MySQL convention.\n\n#### Partial / Conditional Indexes\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite\nCREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_tickets_beads_id ON tickets(beads_id) WHERE beads_id IS NOT NULL;\n\n-- Postgres\nCREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_tickets_beads_id ON tickets(beads_id) WHERE beads_id IS NOT NULL;\n\n-- MySQL: NOT SUPPORTED\n-- Workaround: use a generated column and unique index on the generated column\n```\n\nMySQL does not support `WHERE` clauses on indexes (partial indexes). This is a significant limitation. The workaround is to use generated columns or to enforce uniqueness at the application level.\n\n#### ON DELETE CASCADE\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite: enforced when PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON\nFOREIGN KEY (tenant_id) REFERENCES agent_tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n\n-- Postgres: enforced by default\nFOREIGN KEY (tenant_id) REFERENCES agent_tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n\n-- MySQL: enforced when the storage engine supports it (InnoDB does)\nFOREIGN KEY (tenant_id) REFERENCES agent_tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n```\n\nAll three backends support `ON DELETE CASCADE` with InnoDB (MySQL's default engine). **PlanetScale and Vitess-based MySQL deployments do not support foreign keys.** If you target PlanetScale, you must handle referential integrity at the application layer.\n\n---\n\n## Part 3: Porting to MySQL — A Practical Guide\n\n### Chapter 6: Local MySQL Container Setup\n\nBefore writing any code, get a MySQL instance running locally.\n\n#### Docker Compose Configuration\n\nCreate a `docker-compose.mysql.yml` in the project root:\n\n```yaml\nversion: \"3.9\"\nservices:\n  mysql:\n    image: mysql:8.4\n    container_name: bchat-mysql\n    environment:\n      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: rootpass\n      MYSQL_DATABASE: memos\n      MYSQL_USER: memos\n      MYSQL_PASSWORD: memospass\n    ports:\n      - \"3306:3306\"\n    volumes:\n      - mysql_data:/var/lib/mysql\n    command: >\n      --default-authentication-plugin=mysql_native_password\n      --log-bin-trust-function-creators=1\n\nvolumes:\n  mysql_data:\n```\n\nStart it:\n\n```bash\ndocker compose -f docker-compose.mysql.yml up -d\n```\n\nVerify connectivity:\n\n```bash\nmysql -h 127.0.0.1 -u memos -pmemospass memos -e \"SELECT VERSION();\"\n```\n\n#### Environment Variables for MySQL Mode\n\n```bash\nexport MEMOS_DRIVER=mysql\nexport MEMOS_DSN=\"memos:memospass@tcp(127.0.0.1:3306)/memos?charset=utf8mb4&parseTime=true&loc=UTC\"\n```\n\nNote the `parseTime=true` parameter — this tells the Go MySQL driver to automatically scan `TIMESTAMP`/`DATETIME` columns into `time.Time` values. Without it, timestamps are returned as strings.\n\n#### Testing MySQL 9.0\n\nReplace the image with `mysql:9.0` for testing with the latest MySQL. The SQL dialect changes between 8.0 and 9.0 are minimal for the operations we need, but 9.0 removes some deprecated features (like `GROUP BY` ASC/DESC shorthand that was already removed in 8.0.13).\n\n#### Testing PlanetScale Compatibility\n\nPlanetScale uses Vitess, which is MySQL-compatible but has significant differences:\n\n- No foreign keys (Vitess ignores them)\n- No CHECK constraints (Vitess ignores them)\n- No `LOCK TABLES` (Vitess uses distributed locks)\n- No `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` with more complex expressions\n- Limited DDL (some ALTER TABLE operations require online schema changes via `vtctl`)\n- No `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` across shards\n\nTo test PlanetScale compatibility, you would need a PlanetScale database or a Vitess instance. For local testing, PlanetScale provides a CLI (`pscale connect`) that opens a local TCP tunnel to your database branch.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 7: Writing MySQL Agent Migrations\n\nNow we port the missing migrations. Start with version `0.26` and work through `0.31`.\n\n#### Migration File Structure\n\nEach migration file goes in `store/migration/mysql/`:\n\n```\nstore/migration/mysql/\n├── 0.26/\n│   ├── 00__agent_tenants.sql\n│   ├── 01__agent_audiences.sql\n│   ├── 02__agent_services.sql\n│   ├── 03__agent_exclusions.sql\n│   └── ...\n├── 0.27/\n│   ├── 00__rbac.sql\n│   └── ...\n├── 0.28/\n│   ├── 00__simulations.sql\n│   └── ...\n├── 0.29/\n│   ├── 00__scripts.sql\n│   └── ...\n├── 0.30/\n│   ├── 00__bridge.sql\n│   └── ...\n└── 0.31/\n    ├── 00__integrations.sql\n    └── 01__events.sql\n```\n\n#### Translating SQLite DDL to MySQL\n\nLet's walk through a specific example: the `agent_tenants` table.\n\n**SQLite version** (from `store/migration/sqlite/0.26/00__agent_tenants.sql`):\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE agent_tenants (\n    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,\n    slug TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,\n    company_name TEXT NOT NULL,\n    guid TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,\n    widget_key TEXT,\n    vertical TEXT,\n    is_active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,\n    processing_options TEXT,\n    allowed_domains TEXT,\n    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,\n    updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP\n);\n\nCREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_agent_tenants_guid ON agent_tenants(guid);\nCREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_agent_tenants_widget_key ON agent_tenants(widget_key);\n```\n\n**MySQL translation:**\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE `agent_tenants` (\n    `id` INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,\n    `slug` VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,\n    `company_name` VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,\n    `guid` VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,\n    `widget_key` VARCHAR(255) DEFAULT NULL,\n    `vertical` VARCHAR(100) DEFAULT NULL,\n    `is_active` BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,\n    `processing_options` JSON DEFAULT NULL,\n    `allowed_domains` JSON DEFAULT NULL,\n    `created_at` TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,\n    `updated_at` TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,\n    UNIQUE KEY `uk_agent_tenants_slug` (`slug`),\n    UNIQUE KEY `uk_agent_tenants_guid` (`guid`)\n) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4 COLLATE=utf8mb4_unicode_ci;\n\nCREATE INDEX `idx_agent_tenants_guid` ON `agent_tenants`(`guid`);\nCREATE INDEX `idx_agent_tenants_widget_key` ON `agent_tenants`(`widget_key`);\n```\n\n**Key changes:**\n\n| SQLite | MySQL | Why |\n|--------|-------|-----|\n| `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` | `INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY` | MySQL's auto-increment syntax |\n| `TEXT` | `VARCHAR(255)` or `TEXT` | VARCHAR for indexed columns (MySQL limits index key length), TEXT for large blobs |\n| `UNIQUE` constraint on column | `UNIQUE KEY` at table level | Both work, but table-level UNIQUE KEY is more explicit |\n| `DEFAULT 1` (integer) | `DEFAULT TRUE` (boolean) | MySQL BOOLEAN is TINYINT, but TRUE/FALSE is idiomatic |\n| No ENGINE/CHARSET | `ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4` | Required for foreign key support and full Unicode |\n\n#### Handling JSON Columns\n\nThe SQLite schema uses `TEXT` for JSON fields like `processing_options` and `allowed_domains`. In MySQL, use the `JSON` type:\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite (stores as TEXT)\nprocessing_options TEXT,\n\n-- MySQL (validates as JSON)\nprocessing_options JSON DEFAULT NULL,\n```\n\nMySQL's `JSON` type validates the JSON on insert and stores it in a binary format. This is stricter than SQLite's TEXT approach but prevents malformed JSON from entering the database.\n\n#### Handling TIMESTAMP vs BIGINT\n\nThe SQLite agent tables use `TIMESTAMP` type with `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` default. Some tables use `BIGINT` epoch timestamps. The MySQL equivalents:\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite: TIMESTAMP default\ncreated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP\n\n-- MySQL: same syntax, works the same\ncreated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP\n\n-- SQLite: BIGINT epoch\ncreated_ts BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%s', 'now'))\n\n-- MySQL: BIGINT epoch equivalent\ncreated_ts BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT (UNIX_TIMESTAMP())\n```\n\n**Consistency choice:** The existing MySQL core tables use `TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`. I recommend using the same approach for agent tables to remain consistent with the existing MySQL style. This means your Go code will scan `time.Time` values from the database (with `parseTime=true` in the DSN).\n\n#### Handling Foreign Keys\n\n**SQLite:**\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE agent_audiences (\n    tenant_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES agent_tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,\n    ...\n);\n```\n\n**MySQL (with InnoDB):**\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE `agent_audiences` (\n    `tenant_id` INT NOT NULL,\n    ...\n    CONSTRAINT `fk_audience_tenant` FOREIGN KEY (`tenant_id`) REFERENCES `agent_tenants`(`id`) ON DELETE CASCADE\n) ENGINE=InnoDB;\n```\n\n**PlanetScale/Vitess warning:** When targeting PlanetScale, you must remove all foreign key constraints because Vitess does not support them. Replace them with application-level referential integrity checks.\n\n#### Discretionary Content: TINYINT vs BOOLEAN for SQLite Integer Booleans\n\nSQLite uses `INTEGER` for booleans: `is_active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1`. MySQL prefers `BOOLEAN` (which is `TINYINT(1)` under the hood):\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite pattern\nis_active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,\nCHECK (is_active IN (0, 1))\n\n-- MySQL pattern\nis_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,\n```\n\nThe Go code in SQLite scans these as `int` and checks `isActive == 1`. In MySQL, `BOOLEAN` values come back from `database/sql` as `bool` if you scan into a `bool` variable, or as `int64` (0 or 1) if you scan into an `int`.\n\n#### CHECK Constraints in MySQL\n\nIf targeting MySQL 8.0.16+ or 8.4/9.0:\n\n```sql\nstatus TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'processing', 'completed', 'failed'))\n```\n\nMySQL 8.0.16+ enforces CHECK constraints. If targeting older versions or PlanetScale, remove the CHECK and validate in Go code.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 8: Implementing MySQL Agent Methods\n\nOnce the migrations are written, implement the Go store methods. The good news: **SQLite and MySQL use the same placeholder syntax (`?`) and the same `LastInsertId()` pattern.** This means you can copy the SQLite implementation and only adjust:\n\n1. Timestamp functions (`CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` vs `strftime`)\n2. UPSERT syntax (`ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` vs `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`)\n3. Identifier quoting (backticks vs no quotes)\n4. Column types in Scan (bool vs int for booleans)\n\n#### Step-by-Step: Porting CreateAgentIntegration\n\n**SQLite implementation** (`store/db/sqlite/agent.go:2600`):\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) CreateAgentIntegration(ctx context.Context, integration *store.AgentIntegration) (*store.AgentIntegration, error) {\n    stmt := `\n        INSERT INTO agent_integrations (tenant_id, integration_type, label, config, is_active, created_at, updated_at)\n        VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER), CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER))\n    `\n    result, err := d.db.ExecContext(ctx, stmt,\n        integration.TenantID, integration.IntegrationType, integration.Label,\n        integration.Config, integration.IsActive,\n    )\n    if err != nil {\n        return nil, fmt.Errorf(\"failed to create agent integration: %w\", err)\n    }\n    id, err := result.LastInsertId()\n    if err != nil {\n        return nil, fmt.Errorf(\"failed to get last insert id: %w\", err)\n    }\n    integration.ID = int32(id)\n    return integration, nil\n}\n```\n\n**MySQL implementation:**\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) CreateAgentIntegration(ctx context.Context, integration *store.AgentIntegration) (*store.AgentIntegration, error) {\n    stmt := `\n        INSERT INTO ` + \"`agent_integrations`\" + ` (` + \"`tenant_id`, `integration_type`, `label`, `config`, `is_active`, `created_at`, `updated_at`\" + `)\n        VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, NOW(), NOW())\n    `\n    result, err := d.db.ExecContext(ctx, stmt,\n        integration.TenantID, integration.IntegrationType, integration.Label,\n        integration.Config, integration.IsActive,\n    )\n    if err != nil {\n        return nil, fmt.Errorf(\"failed to create agent integration: %w\", err)\n    }\n    id, err := result.LastInsertId()\n    if err != nil {\n        return nil, fmt.Errorf(\"failed to get last insert id: %w\", err)\n    }\n    integration.ID = int32(id)\n    return integration, nil\n}\n```\n\n**Changes:**\n1. `CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER)` → `NOW()` (MySQL native timestamp function)\n2. Added backtick quotes around identifiers (MySQL convention)\n3. Everything else is identical — same placeholders, same `LastInsertId()`, same error handling\n\n#### Step-by-Step: Porting GetAgentIntegration\n\n**SQLite:**\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) GetAgentIntegration(ctx context.Context, find *store.FindAgentIntegration) (*store.AgentIntegration, error) {\n    query := \"SELECT id, tenant_id, integration_type, label, config, is_active, created_at, updated_at FROM agent_integrations WHERE 1=1\"\n    args := []any{}\n    if find.ID != nil {\n        query += \" AND id = ?\"\n        args = append(args, *find.ID)\n    }\n    if find.TenantID != nil {\n        query += \" AND tenant_id = ?\"\n        args = append(args, *find.TenantID)\n    }\n    // ...\n    var integration store.AgentIntegration\n    var isActive int\n    err := d.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, query, args...).Scan(\n        &integration.ID, &integration.TenantID, &integration.IntegrationType,\n        &integration.Label, &integration.Config, &isActive,\n        &integration.CreatedAt, &integration.UpdatedAt,\n    )\n    integration.IsActive = isActive == 1\n    return &integration, nil\n}\n```\n\n**MySQL:**\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) GetAgentIntegration(ctx context.Context, find *store.FindAgentIntegration) (*store.AgentIntegration, error) {\n    query := \"SELECT `id`, `tenant_id`, `integration_type`, `label`, `config`, `is_active`, `created_at`, `updated_at` FROM `agent_integrations` WHERE 1=1\"\n    args := []any{}\n    if find.ID != nil {\n        query += \" AND `id` = ?\"\n        args = append(args, *find.ID)\n    }\n    if find.TenantID != nil {\n        query += \" AND `tenant_id` = ?\"\n        args = append(args, *find.TenantID)\n    }\n    // ...\n    var integration store.AgentIntegration\n    var isActive bool\n    err := d.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, query, args...).Scan(\n        &integration.ID, &integration.TenantID, &integration.IntegrationType,\n        &integration.Label, &integration.Config, &isActive,\n        &integration.CreatedAt, &integration.UpdatedAt,\n    )\n    integration.IsActive = isActive\n    return &integration, nil\n}\n```\n\n**Changes:**\n1. Added backtick quotes\n2. `var isActive int` → `var isActive bool` (MySQL BOOLEAN columns can be scanned into bool)\n3. `integration.IsActive = isActive == 1` → `integration.IsActive = isActive` (bool assignment)\n\n#### Step-by-Step: Porting UPSERT (Rate Limiting)\n\n**SQLite** uses `ON CONFLICT`:\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) GetOrCreateAgentRateLimit(ctx context.Context, tenantID int32, audienceType, clientIP string) (*store.AgentRateLimit, error) {\n    stmt := `\n        INSERT INTO agent_rate_limits (tenant_id, audience_type, client_ip, request_count, window_start)\n        VALUES (?, ?, ?, 0, CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER))\n        ON CONFLICT(tenant_id, audience_type, client_ip) DO NOTHING\n    `\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\n**MySQL:**\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) GetOrCreateAgentRateLimit(ctx context.Context, tenantID int32, audienceType, clientIP string) (*store.AgentRateLimit, error) {\n    stmt := `\n        INSERT INTO ` + \"`agent_rate_limits`\" + ` (` + \"`tenant_id`, `audience_type`, `client_ip`, `request_count`, `window_start`\" + `)\n        VALUES (?, ?, ?, 0, UNIX_TIMESTAMP())\n        ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE ` + \"`id`\" + ` = ` + \"`id`\" + `\n    `\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\nThe `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = id` is a no-op update — it ensures the row exists without incrementing the counter. For the increment operation:\n\n```sql\n-- MySQL increment\nUPDATE `agent_rate_limits`\nSET `request_count` = `request_count` + 1\nWHERE `tenant_id` = ? AND `audience_type` = ? AND `client_ip` = ?;\n```\n\n#### The Bridge Delivery System: Skip or Port?\n\nThe bridge delivery system in `store/db/mysql/bridge.go` currently returns `store.ErrBridgeUnsupportedDatabase` for every method, and `SupportsBridgeDelivery()` returns `false`. The service layer checks this before calling bridge methods.\n\nFor a first porting pass, you have two options:\n\n1. **Keep it unsupported.** The service layer handles this gracefully by checking `SupportsBridgeDelivery()`. Users of MySQL simply cannot use the bridge integration feature.\n\n2. **Port it.** The bridge delivery system uses an outbox pattern with claim-based delivery. This requires implementing `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and complex state machine transitions. It's a significant effort.\n\n**Recommendation:** Keep bridge delivery unsupported for the first porting pass. Mark it as `TODO` and move on to the higher-priority agent features. Bridge delivery is a premium feature; MySQL users may not need it.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 9: DBaaS Deployment Considerations\n\nDifferent MySQL-based database services have different compatibility profiles. Here is how to target each one.\n\n#### Plain MySQL (8.4 / 9.0)\n\nFull compatibility. Use all MySQL features: foreign keys, CHECK constraints, JSON type, `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`. This is the simplest target.\n\n#### PlanetScale (Vitess)\n\nPlanetScale runs Vitess. Key limitations:\n\n- **No foreign keys.** Remove all `REFERENCES` and `ON DELETE CASCADE`. Handle referential integrity in Go code.\n- **No CHECK constraints.** Validate in Go code.\n- **Limited DDL.** Many `ALTER TABLE` operations require online schema changes. PlanetScale uses `vtctl` for DDL, not raw SQL. You may need to use PlanetScale's deploy request workflow for schema changes.\n- **No `LOCK TABLES`.** Use optimistic locking or application-level mutexes.\n- **No `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` across shards.** Only works within a single shard.\n- **Index limitations.** Maximum index key length is 768 bytes (for `utf8mb4`).\n\nFor PlanetScale, your `agent_tenants` table would look like:\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE `agent_tenants` (\n    `id` INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,\n    `slug` VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,\n    `company_name` VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,\n    `guid` VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,\n    `widget_key` VARCHAR(255) DEFAULT NULL,\n    `vertical` VARCHAR(100) DEFAULT NULL,\n    `is_active` BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,\n    `processing_options` JSON DEFAULT NULL,\n    `allowed_domains` JSON DEFAULT NULL,\n    `created_at` TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,\n    `updated_at` TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,\n    UNIQUE KEY `uk_agent_tenants_slug` (`slug`),\n    UNIQUE KEY `uk_agent_tenants_guid` (`guid`)\n) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4;\n\n-- No foreign key on agent_audiences.tenant_id — enforced in Go.\n```\n\nAnd the `agent_events` table (which would otherwise have foreign keys to `agent_integrations` and `agent_tenants`):\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE `agent_events` (\n    `id` INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,\n    `tenant_id` INT NOT NULL,\n    `integration_id` INT NOT NULL,\n    `event_type` VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,\n    `payload` JSON NOT NULL,\n    `status` VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',\n    `created_at` TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP\n    -- No FOREIGN KEY constraints\n);\n```\n\n#### TiDB\n\nTiDB is MySQL-compatible at the SQL level with some differences:\n\n- Foreign keys are supported but not enforced by default (set `foreign_key_checks=1` or use TiDB 6.6+ which supports them)\n- CHECK constraints are parsed but not enforced (as of TiDB 7.x)\n- JSON type is supported\n- `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` is supported\n- No `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` across regions (TiDB uses optimistic transactions by default)\n- Auto-increment works but is not guaranteed to be sequential (TiDB allocates batches)\n\nTiDB is closer to MySQL compatibility than PlanetScale but still has enough differences to warrant a separate testing pass.\n\n#### Choosing Your Target\n\nIf you are porting MySQL support for a specific customer or deployment, target their specific platform. If you want broad MySQL compatibility, target **plain MySQL 8.4** and document which features break on PlanetScale and TiDB.\n\n---\n\n## Part 4: Operations Engineering\n\n### Chapter 10: Migration Strategy\n\nThe bchat migration system uses Go's `embed.FS` to bundle SQL files with the binary. Migrations are versioned per directory:\n\n```go\n//go:embed migration\nvar migrationFS embed.FS\n\nfunc (s *Store) getMigrationBasePath() string {\n    return fmt.Sprintf(\"migration/%s/\", s.profile.Driver)\n}\n```\n\nWhen the application starts, it:\n1. Checks existing migration history in the database\n2. Discovers migration files in the embedded FS\n3. Applies any files with versions higher than the latest applied\n4. If no migration history exists, applies `LATEST.sql` (the full schema)\n\n#### Adding MySQL to the Migration System\n\nSince MySQL migrations are in a separate directory (`store/migration/mysql/`), adding them is straightforward:\n1. Create the migration directories (0.26–0.31)\n2. Write the SQL files\n3. Update `LATEST.sql` to include all new tables\n4. The Go code automatically discovers them via `embed.FS`\n\nNo changes to the migrator code are needed. The migrator already supports MySQL via the `profile.Driver` path.\n\n#### Schema Drift Detection\n\nWhen adding MySQL migrations, you need a way to verify that the MySQL schema matches the SQLite/Postgres schema (for the same version). Without this check, it's easy to miss a table or column.\n\n**Option A: Manual review.** Compare the SQL files side-by-side. This is what the existing codebase does.\n\n**Option B: Automated schema comparison.** Use a tool like `go-migrate`'s diff or `atlasgo` to compare schemas:\n\n```bash\n# Compare SQLite and MySQL schemas\natlas schema diff \\\n  --from \"sqlite://build/data/memos_dev.db\" \\\n  --to \"mysql://memos:memospass@localhost:3306/memos\" \\\n  --dev-url \"docker://sqlite/development\"\n```\n\n**Option C: CI check.** In CI, spin up SQLite and MySQL containers, run migrations on both, then diff the schemas:\n\n```yaml\n# .github/workflows/schema-parity.yml (conceptual)\njobs:\n  schema-parity:\n    services:\n      mysql:\n        image: mysql:8.4\n        env:\n          MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: rootpass\n          MYSQL_DATABASE: memos\n    steps:\n      - run: ./build/memos --mode dev --driver mysql --dsn \"root:rootpass@tcp(mysql:3306)/memos\"\n      - run: ./build/memos --mode dev --driver sqlite --data /tmp/data\n      - run: |\n          sqlite3 /tmp/data/memos_dev.db .schema > /tmp/sqlite_schema.sql\n          mysqldump --no-data -h mysql -u root -prootpass memos > /tmp/mysql_schema.sql\n          # Diff the two schemas (excluding engine-specific types)\n```\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 11: Testing Multi-Backend\n\nRunning the same test suite against SQLite, Postgres, and MySQL is the only way to ensure parity.\n\n#### Test Architecture\n\nThe current test setup is described in `store/test/README.md`. The approach is:\n\n1. Define the test suite once (using the `store.Driver` interface)\n2. Run the suite against each backend\n3. Use environment variables to select the backend\n\nFor MySQL specifically:\n\n```go\nfunc TestAgentIntegrationMySQL(t *testing.T) {\n    dsn := os.Getenv(\"MYSQL_TEST_DSN\")\n    if dsn == \"\" {\n        t.Skip(\"MYSQL_TEST_DSN not set\")\n    }\n    db, err := mysql.NewDB(&profile.Profile{\n        Driver: \"mysql\",\n        DSN:    dsn,\n    })\n    if err != nil {\n        t.Fatalf(\"failed to create MySQL driver: %v\", err)\n    }\n    defer db.Close()\n\n    // Run the common test suite\n    RunAgentIntegrationTests(t, db)\n}\n```\n\n#### Testcontainers for MySQL\n\nFor CI without a persistent MySQL instance, use `testcontainers-go`:\n\n```go\nimport (\n    \"github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go\"\n    \"github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go/wait\"\n)\n\nfunc setupMySQLContainer(t *testing.T) (string, func()) {\n    ctx := context.Background()\n    req := testcontainers.ContainerRequest{\n        Image:        \"mysql:8.4\",\n        ExposedPorts: []string{\"3306/tcp\"},\n        Env: map[string]string{\n            \"MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD\": \"test\",\n            \"MYSQL_DATABASE\":      \"memos_test\",\n        },\n        WaitingFor: wait.ForLog(\"port: 3306  MySQL Community Server\"),\n    }\n    mysqlC, err := testcontainers.GenericContainer(ctx, testcontainers.GenericContainerRequest{\n        ContainerRequest: req,\n        Started:          true,\n    })\n    // ...\n    port, _ := mysqlC.MappedPort(ctx, \"3306\")\n    dsn := fmt.Sprintf(\"root:test@tcp(localhost:%s)/memos_test?parseTime=true&multiStatements=true\", port.Port())\n    return dsn, func() { mysqlC.Terminate(ctx) }\n}\n```\n\n#### What to Test\n\nFor each agent method, test:\n\n1. **Create** — insert a row, verify it returns with an ID\n2. **Read** — retrieve by ID, by tenant, by other find fields\n3. **Update** — modify a row, verify the change\n4. **Delete** — remove a row, verify it's gone\n5. **Cascade** — delete a parent (tenant), verify children are removed (CASCADE)\n6. **Duplicate** — attempt to insert a duplicate, verify the unique constraint fires\n7. **Not found** — query for a nonexistent ID, verify nil/error is returned\n\n#### Common Pitfalls Across Backends\n\n| Pitfall | SQLite | Postgres | MySQL |\n|---------|--------|----------|-------|\n| Timezone | Stores UTC epoch | Stores UTC epoch | Stores in session timezone |\n| Integer overflow | No limit (64-bit) | INT is 32-bit, BIGINT is 64-bit | INT is 32-bit, BIGINT is 64-bit |\n| String truncation | No | No | Yes (strict mode) |\n| Float precision | REAL is 64-bit | DOUBLE PRECISION is 64-bit | DOUBLE is 64-bit |\n| Transaction isolation | SERIALIZABLE by default | READ COMMITTED by default | REPEATABLE READ by default |\n\nFor MySQL, **string truncation** is the most common surprise. In strict mode (default since MySQL 5.7), inserting a string longer than `VARCHAR(255)` into a `VARCHAR(255)` column raises an error. In SQLite and Postgres, longer strings are accepted (up to other limits). When porting, ensure your VARCHAR lengths accommodate the maximum possible input.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 12: Production Readiness Checklist\n\nWhen MySQL support moves from \"works in dev\" to \"production-ready\", verify each item:\n\n#### Connection Pooling\n\n```go\n// Default values — tune for your workload\ndriver.db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)\ndriver.db.SetMaxIdleConns(10)\ndriver.db.SetConnMaxLifetime(5 * time.Minute)\ndriver.db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(1 * time.Minute)\n```\n\nThe MySQL driver uses TCP connections by default. Connection pooling is critical for performance. The existing SQLite implementation uses a file handle (one connection), and Postgres uses TCP with pooling. MySQL should be configured similarly to Postgres.\n\n#### Migration Locking\n\nWhen multiple instances start simultaneously, they may attempt to run migrations concurrently. SQLite uses file-level locking. Postgres uses advisory locks. MySQL uses `GET_LOCK()`:\n\n```go\n// MySQL migration lock\nfunc (d *DB) acquireMigrationLock(ctx context.Context) (func() error, error) {\n    var result int\n    err := d.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, \"SELECT GET_LOCK('memos_migration', 30)\").Scan(&result)\n    if err != nil || result != 1 {\n        return nil, fmt.Errorf(\"failed to acquire migration lock\")\n    }\n    return func() error {\n        _, err := d.db.ExecContext(ctx, \"SELECT RELEASE_LOCK('memos_migration')\")\n        return err\n    }, nil\n}\n```\n\n#### Backup and Restore\n\n```bash\n# SQLite backup\nsqlite3 /path/to/memos_dev.db \".backup /backup/memos_$(date +%Y%m%d).db\"\n\n# MySQL backup (with native webhook tables)\nmysqldump -h localhost -u memos -p --routines --triggers memos > /backup/memos_$(date +%Y%m%d).sql\n\n# Restore\nmysql -h localhost -u memos -p memos < /backup/memos_20260711.sql\n```\n\n#### Monitoring\n\nFor MySQL production, monitor:\n\n- `SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST` — long-running queries\n- `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` — deadlocks and transaction contention\n- Slow query log (configured via MySQL's `long_query_time` setting)\n- Connection pool metrics (via `db.Stats()` in Go)\n\n#### Performance Comparison\n\n| Operation | SQLite (WAL) | Postgres (local) | MySQL (local) |\n|-----------|-------------|------------------|---------------|\n| Concurrent reads | Excellent | Excellent | Excellent |\n| Concurrent writes | Poor (single writer) | Excellent | Good |\n| Connection overhead | None (file-based) | Moderate (TCP) | Moderate (TCP) |\n| Read latency (small) | ~1μs | ~100μs | ~100μs |\n| Write latency | ~10μs | ~100μs | ~100μs |\n\nFor the agent event system (bugs/033), the event claiming mechanism requires **row-level locking** (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or atomic `UPDATE` with status check). All three backends support this, but SQLite's single-writer model means event claims are effectively serialized (which is fine for the event polling pattern used in this codebase).\n\n---\n\n## Part 5: The bugs/033 Lens — Database Parity and Webhook Events\n\n### Chapter 13: What bugs/033 Requires from the Database\n\nThe bugs/033 feature (Native Webhook Integrations v1) adds two database tables and five store methods that **must** work for the feature to function:\n\n#### Tables\n\n**`agent_integrations`** — stores webhook integration configuration:\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE agent_integrations (\n    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,\n    tenant_id INTEGER NOT NULL,\n    integration_type TEXT NOT NULL,     -- 'webhook', 'slack', etc.\n    label TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',\n    config TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',   -- JSON: url, secret, headers, etc.\n    is_active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,\n    created_at BIGINT NOT NULL,\n    updated_at BIGINT NOT NULL,\n    FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id) REFERENCES agent_tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n);\nCREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_agent_integrations_tenant_type\n    ON agent_integrations(tenant_id, integration_type);\n```\n\n**`agent_events`** — stores webhook event queue entries:\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE agent_events (\n    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,\n    tenant_id INTEGER NOT NULL,\n    integration_id INTEGER NOT NULL,\n    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,            -- 'message_created', 'lead_captured', etc.\n    payload TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',  -- JSON event payload\n    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'processing',\n    claimed_at BIGINT DEFAULT NULL,\n    attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,\n    last_error TEXT DEFAULT NULL,\n    idempotency_key TEXT UNIQUE,\n    created_at BIGINT NOT NULL,\n    FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id) REFERENCES agent_tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,\n    FOREIGN KEY (integration_id) REFERENCES agent_integrations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n);\nCREATE INDEX idx_agent_events_status ON agent_events(status);\nCREATE INDEX idx_agent_events_claimed ON agent_events(claimed_at);\n```\n\n#### Store Methods\n\nThe five store methods that bugs/033 requires:\n\n```go\nCreateAgentIntegration(ctx, integration) (*AgentIntegration, error)\nGetAgentIntegration(ctx, find) (*AgentIntegration, error)\nListAgentIntegrations(ctx, find) ([]*AgentIntegration, error)\nUpdateAgentIntegration(ctx, update) error\nDeleteAgentIntegration(ctx, id) error\n\nCreateAgentEvent(ctx, event) (*AgentEvent, error)\nListAgentEvents(ctx, find) ([]*AgentEvent, error)\nClaimPendingEvents(ctx, limit) ([]*AgentEvent, error)\nUpdateAgentEvent(ctx, update) error\n```\n\n#### The Event Claiming Pattern\n\n`ClaimPendingEvents` is the most interesting method. It implements a claim-based worker pattern:\n\n```sql\n-- SQLite implementation\nUPDATE agent_events\nSET status = 'processing',\n    claimed_at = CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER),\n    attempts = attempts + 1\nWHERE id IN (\n    SELECT id FROM agent_events\n    WHERE status IN ('pending', 'failed')\n      AND (claimed_at IS NULL OR claimed_at < CAST(strftime('%s','now') AS INTEGER) - 60)\n    ORDER BY created_at ASC\n    LIMIT ?\n);\n```\n\nThis concurrently-safe pattern ensures that:\n- Only one worker claims each event\n- Failed events are retried after a 60-second cooldown\n- Events are processed in FIFO order\n- The subquery avoids race conditions (in SQLite's serialized writer model)\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 14: Why MySQL Isn't Ready for bugs/033\n\nIf you switch bchat to MySQL and try to use the webhook integration feature, here is exactly what breaks:\n\n#### 1. Missing Tables → Handler Returns 500\n\nWhen the handler calls `ListAgentIntegrations`, it first creates the table... wait, no — it calls `GetAgentIntegration`, which returns `errNotImplemented`:\n\n```go\n// HTTP handler\nfunc (h *Handler) ListIntegrations(c echo.Context) error {\n    tenantID := getTenantFromContext(c)\n    integrations, err := h.store.ListAgentIntegrations(c.Request().Context(), &store.FindAgentIntegration{\n        TenantID: tenantID,\n    })\n    if err != nil {\n        return echo.NewHTTPError(http.StatusInternalServerError, \"Failed to list integrations\")\n    }\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\nThe MySQL stub returns `errNotImplemented`, which is a non-nil error. The handler returns 500. The user sees an internal server error.\n\nEven if the handler were more graceful, the real problem is that the `agent_integrations` table doesn't exist in the MySQL schema. If a MySQL migration were applied, the `CREATE TABLE` would fail because the referenced `agent_tenants` table doesn't exist either. The chain of failure cascades.\n\n#### 2. Fail-Open Rate Limiting → Security Gap\n\nWithout working rate limiting, the webhook delivery system can be flooded. The MySQL driver's fail-open behavior logs a warning but allows all requests:\n\n```go\n// User sees: 200 OK for every request\n// Operator sees: \"agent rate limit check not implemented for MySQL, allowing request\"\n// Attacker sees: unlimited requests\n```\n\nIn the context of webhook delivery, this means a compromised tenant could:\n- Queue unlimited events (resource exhaustion)\n- Deliver events faster than the webhook endpoint can handle (outgoing DDoS)\n- Bypass per-tenant rate limits intended for fair resource allocation\n\n#### 3. Silent Stub Data Loss\n\nIf any code path calls `CreateAgentWorkflow` (which the webhook event processing might, for tracking purposes), the MySQL stub returns `nil, nil`. The caller receives no error and no data. If the caller checks for `nil` result and skips processing, the workflow is silently dropped.\n\n#### 4. Bridge Unsupported → No External Delivery\n\nIf the webhook event processing uses the bridge delivery system for external communication, the MySQL backend returns `ErrBridgeUnsupportedDatabase`. The service layer checks `SupportsBridgeDelivery()` and skips bridge operations, but the webhook delivery itself runs on a different code path (direct HTTP callout, not bridge). The bridge limitation affects the separate messaging bridge feature, not the webhook integration directly.\n\nHowever, if the architecture evolves to use the bridge outbox pattern for webhook delivery (which would be a natural evolution), MySQL would be unable to participate.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 15: Porting Order — What to Implement First\n\nIf you want to make bugs/033 work on MySQL, here is the implementation order:\n\n#### Priority 1: Schema (Hours)\n\nCreate MySQL migrations for all tables that bugs/033 depends on, transitively:\n\n1. `agent_tenants` (dependency of everything)\n2. `agent_audiences` (runtime dependency of agent sessions)\n3. `agent_sessions` (used by event creation paths)\n4. `agent_integrations` (the feature's primary table)\n5. `agent_events` (the feature's queue table)\n\nYou don't need ALL agent tables for bugs/033 to work — just the ones in the dependency chain. Tables like `agent_observations`, `agent_workflows`, and `bridge_*` can wait.\n\n#### Priority 2: Tenant CRUD (Days)\n\nImplement the tenant, audience, and session methods that the integration and event operations depend on:\n\n```go\nCreateAgentTenant, GetAgentTenant, ListAgentTenants\nCreateAgentAudience, GetAgentAudience, ListAgentAudiences\nCreateAgentSession, GetAgentSession\n```\n\nThese are straightforward CRUD translations from SQLite. Without these, the integration create handler fails because it needs a valid tenant context.\n\n#### Priority 3: Integration CRUD (Days)\n\nImplement the five integration store methods:\n\n```go\nCreateAgentIntegration, GetAgentIntegration\nListAgentIntegrations, UpdateAgentIntegration, DeleteAgentIntegration\n```\n\nThese directly enable the \"Create Webhook\" and \"List Webhooks\" UI screens. Without these, the feature doesn't exist for the user.\n\n#### Priority 4: Event CRUD + ClaimPendingEvents (Critical — Days)\n\nImplement the event store methods, including the most critical one: `ClaimPendingEvents`.\n\n```sql\n-- MySQL implementation of ClaimPendingEvents\nUPDATE `agent_events`\nSET `status` = 'processing',\n    `claimed_at` = NOW(),\n    `attempts` = `attempts` + 1\nWHERE `id` IN (\n    SELECT `id` FROM `agent_events`\n    WHERE `status` IN ('pending', 'failed')\n      AND (`claimed_at` IS NULL OR `claimed_at` < NOW() - INTERVAL 60 SECOND)\n    ORDER BY `created_at` ASC\n    LIMIT ?\n);\n```\n\n**MySQL compatibility note:** MySQL 8.0+ does not support `LIMIT` in subqueries of `UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... LIMIT ?)` in all configurations. You may need to use a different approach:\n\n```sql\n-- Option A: Use a derived table (MySQL 8.0+)\nUPDATE `agent_events`\nSET `status` = 'processing',\n    `claimed_at` = NOW(),\n    `attempts` = `attempts` + 1\nWHERE `id` IN (\n    SELECT `id` FROM (\n        SELECT `id` FROM `agent_events`\n        WHERE `status` IN ('pending', 'failed')\n          AND (`claimed_at` IS NULL OR `claimed_at` < NOW() - INTERVAL 60 SECOND)\n        ORDER BY `created_at` ASC\n        LIMIT ?\n    ) AS `sub`\n);\n```\n\nThe double-nested subquery is a MySQL workaround for the \"can't use LIMIT in subquery of UPDATE\" restriction.\n\n#### Priority 5: Rate Limiting (Security — Days)\n\nReplace the fail-open rate limiter with a real MySQL implementation. The rate limit table needs:\n\n```sql\nCREATE TABLE `agent_rate_limits` (\n    `id` INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,\n    `tenant_id` INT NOT NULL,\n    `audience_type` VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,\n    `client_ip` VARCHAR(45) NOT NULL,\n    `request_count` INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,\n    `window_start` TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,\n    UNIQUE KEY `uk_rate_limit_scope` (`tenant_id`, `audience_type`, `client_ip`)\n);\n```\n\nThe `CheckAndIncrement` method:\n\n```go\nfunc (d *DB) CheckAndIncrementAgentRateLimit(ctx context.Context, tenantID int32, audienceType, clientIP string, rpm int) (bool, error) {\n    // Reset window if expired\n    _, _ = d.db.ExecContext(ctx, `\n        UPDATE `+\"`agent_rate_limits`\"+`\n        SET `+\"`request_count` = 0, `window_start` = NOW()\"+`\n        WHERE `+\"`tenant_id` = ? AND `audience_type` = ? AND `client_ip` = ?\"+`\n          AND `+\"`window_start` < NOW() - INTERVAL 1 MINUTE\"+`\n    `, tenantID, audienceType, clientIP)\n\n    // Increment and check\n    var count int\n    err := d.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, `\n        INSERT INTO `+\"`agent_rate_limits` (`tenant_id`, `audience_type`, `client_ip`, `request_count`, `window_start`)\"+`\n        VALUES (?, ?, ?, 1, NOW())\n        ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE `+\"`request_count` = `request_count` + 1\"+`\n    `, tenantID, audienceType, clientIP).Scan(&count)\n\n    if err == sql.ErrNoRows {\n        // UPSERT succeeded, this is the first request\n        return true, nil\n    }\n\n    // Get current count\n    d.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, `\n        SELECT `+\"`request_count`\"+`\n        FROM `+\"`agent_rate_limits`\"+`\n        WHERE `+\"`tenant_id` = ? AND `audience_type` = ? AND `client_ip` = ?\"+`\n    `, tenantID, audienceType, clientIP).Scan(&count)\n\n    return count <= rpm, nil\n}\n```\n\n**Decision point:** Should rate limiting fail-closed or fail-open when the table doesn't exist? For production, fail-closed is safer. But for development, fail-open makes it easier to test other features before implementing rate limiting. A good middle ground: log a warning and return `true` (allowed) in dev mode, return `false` in prod mode.\n\n#### Priority 6: Everything Else (Weeks to Months)\n\nAfter the critical path for bugs/033 is working, implement the remaining stubs in order of usage frequency:\n\n1. `agent_transcripts` / transcript methods — needed for conversation history\n2. `agent_leads` / lead methods — needed for lead capture\n3. `agent_qa_pairs` — needed for embedding testing\n4. `agent_analysis_results` — needed for conversation analysis\n5. `agent_observations` — needed for observational memory\n6. `bridge_*` — needed for advanced messaging features\n\n---\n\n## Part 6: Architectural Reflections\n\n### Chapter 16: Why Postgres and SQLite Are In Sync But MySQL Lags\n\nThis is not an accident of neglect. There are structural reasons why MySQL parity lags:\n\n#### 1. Historical Evolution\n\nbchat started as a Memos fork, which was SQLite-only. Postgres support was added early in the hosted product development. MySQL was added as a \"nice to have\" third option. The team's focus was on shipping features for the hosted product (Postgres) and local development (SQLite). MySQL was never a deployment target for any paying customer.\n\n#### 2. The pgx/v5 Advantage\n\nPostgres support uses `pgx/v5`, which is a purpose-built Postgres driver with native support for:\n- PostgreSQL-specific types (JSONB, arrays, enums)\n- COPY protocol for bulk operations\n- Prepared statement caching\n- Connection pooling (pgxpool)\n\nThe MySQL driver (`go-sql-driver/mysql`) is more generic. It supports `database/sql` well but doesn't offer Postgres-specific optimizations. The team may have found Postgres more ergonomic for the agent system's JSON-heavy data model.\n\n#### 3. JSON Support\n\nThe agent system stores complex nested data in JSON columns (`payload`, `config`, `guidelines`, `messages`). Postgres's `JSONB` type is excellent for this — it supports indexing, path queries, and partial updates. SQLite stores JSON as `TEXT` (no native JSON operations before 3.38.0). MySQL's `JSON` type is good but was added later (5.7, 2015) and has a learning curve for JSON path expressions.\n\nThe team may have decided that if MySQL parity requires significant JSON workload investment, it should wait until MySQL is a genuine deployment requirement.\n\n#### 4. Migration File Proliferation\n\nEvery new version adds three sets of migration files (SQLite, Postgres, MySQL). The SQLite directory has 32 version directories, Postgres has 14, MySQL has 11. After version 0.25, the MySQL directory stopped growing. This is a common pattern: the initial set of backends is maintained, then one falls behind because there's no automated \"add migration to all backends\" check.\n\n#### 5. CHECK Constraint Fragility\n\nThe SQLite schema uses `CHECK` constraints extensively for data validation. Before MySQL 8.0.16, CHECK constraints were parsed but ignored. The team may have decided that writing MySQL DDL that differs significantly from SQLite/Postgres would be confusing and error-prone.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 17: What a Fourth Backend Would Look Like\n\nIf you were to add a fourth backend (say, CockroachDB or a SQLite clustering solution), the process would be:\n\n1. **Add the driver package** (`store/db/cockroach/agent.go`)\n2. **Implement all ~180 Driver interface methods**\n3. **Create migration directory** (`store/migration/cockroach/`)\n4. **Write migration files** for every version from 0.1 to 0.31\n5. **Update the factory** in `store/db/db.go`\n6. **Add DSN handling** in `internal/profile/profile.go`\n7. **Test** against the fourth backend\n8. **Maintain** parity for all future features\n\nThe cost of adding a fourth backend is roughly:\n- 3–6 months for initial implementation\n- 20–30% more work per new feature (writing the same SQL for four backends)\n- 2x-3x test runtime (running the suite against four backends)\n\n**The abstraction tax:** Every time you add a new store method, you must implement it for every backend. With 180 methods across 3 backends, that's 540 implementations to maintain. A fourth backend would make it 720.\n\nThis is why many projects limit themselves to 2 backends: one for development (SQLite) and one for production (Postgres). The third backend is a significant commitment.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 18: Database Parity as a Business Decision\n\nLet's return to the questions from Chapter 1:\n\n#### When Is Parity Worth It?\n\n| Situation | Decision | Rationale |\n|-----------|----------|-----------|\n| A customer demands MySQL deployment | Port the minimum needed | Only implement what the customer pays for |\n| MySQL is 50%+ of your target market | Full parity | Market requirement |\n| You're building for PlanetScale's ecosystem | MySQL-first, not parity | Target PlanetScale's specific MySQL dialect |\n| You want local dev to match production | SQLite → MySQL parity | Developers on macOS use MySQL in Docker |\n| \"It would be nice to have\" | Don't do it | Opportunity cost is too high |\n\n#### What Is the Cost of Not Porting?\n\n- MySQL users get errors for agent features\n- MySQL users don't get webhook integrations\n- MySQL users are second-class citizens\n- The stubs accumulate more methods over time\n- Technical debt grows, making future porting harder\n\n#### What Is the Cost of Porting?\n\n- Engineering time: 2–6 weeks for full parity\n- Testing infrastructure: CI matrix expansion\n- Maintenance burden: every future feature requires MySQL implementation\n- Documentation: MySQL-specific deployment guides\n- Support: MySQL-related bugs and performance issues\n\n#### The Maturity Model\n\nDatabase parity follows a maturity model:\n\n1. **Single backend** (SQLite only) — No parity concerns, limited deployment\n2. **Dual parity** (SQLite + Postgres) — Local dev + production, manageable\n3. **Triple parity** (SQLite + Postgres + MySQL) — Broad compatibility, high maintenance\n4. **Abstracted** (Any backend via a query builder like SQLBoiler or GORM) — Less control, more flexibility\n\nbchat is at stage 2+ — dual parity for core features, triple parity in the interface but not in practice for agent features.\n\n**Your task in this tutorial is to decide where you want MySQL to sit on this spectrum.** Full parity? Partial parity for bugs/033 features only? Or accept the current stubs and plan for a future porting sprint?\n\n---\n\n## Appendices\n\n### Appendix A: SQL Dialect Reference Card\n\n#### DDL\n\n| Feature | SQLite | Postgres | MySQL |\n|---------|--------|----------|-------|\n| Auto-increment | `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` | `SERIAL PRIMARY KEY` | `INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY` |\n| Big auto-increment | `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` | `BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY` | `BIGINT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY` |\n| Text (short) | `TEXT` | `TEXT` | `VARCHAR(255)` |\n| Text (long) | `TEXT` | `TEXT` | `TEXT` / `LONGTEXT` |\n| Binary | `BLOB` | `BYTEA` | `BLOB` / `MEDIUMBLOB` |\n| JSON | `TEXT` (with app validation) | `JSONB` | `JSON` |\n| Boolean | `INTEGER CHECK(IN 0,1)` | `BOOLEAN` | `BOOLEAN` (TINYINT(1)) |\n| Timestamp (type) | `TEXT` or `INTEGER` | `TIMESTAMPTZ` or `BIGINT` | `TIMESTAMP` or `BIGINT` |\n| Timestamp (now) | `strftime('%s','now')` (epoch) or `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` | `EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM NOW())` (epoch) or `NOW()` | `UNIX_TIMESTAMP()` (epoch) or `NOW()` |\n| Identifier quote | `\"` or none | `\"` | `` ` `` |\n\n#### DML\n\n| Feature | SQLite | Postgres | MySQL |\n|---------|--------|----------|-------|\n| Placeholder | `?` | `$N` | `?` |\n| Return inserted ID | `result.LastInsertId()` | `RETURNING id` | `result.LastInsertId()` |\n| UPSERT | `ON CONFLICT(...) DO UPDATE` | `ON CONFLICT(...) DO UPDATE` | `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` |\n| INSERT IGNORE | `ON CONFLICT(...) DO NOTHING` | `ON CONFLICT(...) DO NOTHING` | `INSERT IGNORE` |\n| LIMIT in subquery | Allowed | Allowed | Needs workaround (derived table) |\n| SELECT FOR UPDATE | Supported (locks entire DB) | Supported (row-level) | Supported (row-level, InnoDB) |\n| Partial index | `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` | `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` | Not supported |\n\n#### Constraints\n\n| Feature | SQLite | Postgres | MySQL |\n|---------|--------|----------|-------|\n| CHECK enforcement | Yes | Yes | Yes (8.0.16+) / Ignored (older) |\n| FK enforcement | Optional (`PRAGMA foreign_keys`) | Always | InnoDB |\n| ON DELETE CASCADE | Yes | Yes | Yes (InnoDB) |\n| UNIQUE constraint | `UNIQUE(col)` | `UNIQUE(col)` | `UNIQUE KEY` or `UNIQUE(col)` |\n| NOT NULL | `col TEXT NOT NULL` | `col TEXT NOT NULL` | `col TEXT NOT NULL` |\n| DEFAULT | `DEFAULT value` | `DEFAULT value` | `DEFAULT value` |\n\n---\n\n### Appendix B: MySQL Porting Checklist\n\nUse this checklist to track your MySQL parity porting progress.\n\n#### ## Complete Ticket Management System Analysis

### 1. TICKET DATA MODEL (`/home/chaschel/Documents/go/bchat/store/ticket.go`)

**Enums:**

```go
type TicketStatus string
const (
    TicketStatusOpen       TicketStatus = "OPEN"
    TicketStatusInProgress TicketStatus = "IN_PROGRESS"
    TicketStatusClosed     TicketStatus = "CLOSED"
)

type TicketPriority string
const (
    TicketPriorityLow    TicketPriority = "LOW"
    TicketPriorityMedium TicketPriority = "MEDIUM"
    TicketPriorityHigh   TicketPriority = "HIGH"
)
```

**Main Struct:**

```go
type Ticket struct {
    ID          int32
    Title       string
    Description string          // Must start with "/m/" (memo link) per Validate()
    Status      TicketStatus
    Priority    TicketPriority
    CreatorID   int32
    AssigneeID  *int32
    CreatedTs   int64
    UpdatedTs   int64
    Type        string          // e.g. "TASK", "BUG", "STORY", "SUPPORT", "agent_escalation"
    Tags        []string        // JSON-encoded in DB, e.g. "escalated"
    TenantID    *int32
}
```

**Validation rule** (line 65-79): `Description` must start with `/m/` -- it is always a link to a Memo. If empty status, defaults to `OPEN`. If empty priority, defaults to `MEDIUM`.

**FindTicket (query filter):**

```go
type FindTicket struct {
    ID          *int32
    CreatorID   *int32
    Type        *string
    Description *string
    TenantID    *int32
    TenantIDs   []int32    // OR semantics for scoped-admin filtering
}
```

**UpdateTicket:**

```go
type UpdateTicket struct {
    ID          int32
    Title       *string
    Description *string
    Status      *TicketStatus
    Priority    *TicketPriority
    AssigneeID  *int32
    UpdatedTs   *int64
    Type        *string
    Tags        []string
}
```

**DeleteTicket:**
```go
type DeleteTicket struct {
    ID int32
}
```

**TicketStore Interface:**

```go
type TicketStore interface {
    CreateTicket(ctx context.Context, ticket *Ticket) (*Ticket, error)
    ListTickets(ctx context.Context, find *FindTicket) ([]*Ticket, error)
    GetTicket(ctx context.Context, find *FindTicket) (*Ticket, error)
    UpdateTicket(ctx context.Context, update *UpdateTicket) (*Ticket, error)
    DeleteTicket(ctx context.Context, delete *DeleteTicket) error
}
```

---

### 2. DATABASE SCHEMA (LATEST.sql - lines 152-181)

```sql
CREATE TABLE tickets (
   id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
   title TEXT NOT NULL,
   description TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
   status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN',
   priority TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'MEDIUM',
   creator_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES user(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
   assignee_id INTEGER REFERENCES user(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
   created_ts BIGINT NOT NULL,
   updated_ts BIGINT NOT NULL,
   type TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'TASK',
   tags TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]',
   beads_id TEXT UNIQUE,
   parent_id INTEGER REFERENCES tickets(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
   labels TEXT DEFAULT '[]',
   dependencies TEXT DEFAULT '[]',
   discovery_context TEXT,
   closed_reason TEXT,
   issue_type TEXT,
   tenant_id INTEGER DEFAULT NULL
);

-- Indexes:
CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_creator_id ON tickets (creator_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_status ON tickets (status);
CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_assignee_id ON tickets (assignee_id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_tickets_beads_id ON tickets(beads_id) WHERE beads_id IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_parent_id ON tickets(parent_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_issue_type ON tickets(issue_type);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_tickets_creator_description_memo ON tickets(creator_id, description) WHERE description LIKE '/m/%';
CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_tenant ON tickets(tenant_id);
```

**Key schema notes:**
- `beads_id` -- unique, nullable, links to Beads issue tracking system
- `parent_id` -- self-referential FK for ticket hierarchies (sub-tickets)
- `labels`, `dependencies` -- JSON arrays
- `discovery_context`, `closed_reason`, `issue_type` -- Beads integration fields
- `tenant_id` -- added in migration 0.27 for multi-tenant isolation
- `(creator_id, description)` partial unique index only when `description LIKE '/m/%'` -- prevents duplicate tickets for the same memo

### 4. TICKET STORE IMPLEMENTATIONS

#### SQLite (`/home/chaschel/Documents/go/bchat/store/db/sqlite/ticket.go` - 239 lines)

**CreateTicket** -- INSERT with `RETURNING id`. Includes all 11 columns. Tags are JSON-marshalled.

**ListTickets** -- Dynamic WHERE builder with these filters:
- `id = ?`
- `creator_id = ?`
- `type = ?`
- `description = ?`
- `tenant_id = ?`
- `tenant_id IN (?, ?, ...)` -- for TenantIDs slice OR-semantics

Always `ORDER BY created_ts DESC`. Returns all 12 columns. Tags are JSON-unmarshalled on read.

**GetTicket** -- Delegates to ListTickets, returns first result or nil.

**UpdateTicket** -- Dynamic SET builder for: title, description, status, priority, assignee_id, updated_ts, type, tags. Uses `RETURNING id, title, description, status, priority, creator_id, assignee_id, created_ts, updated_ts, type, tags, tenant_id` to return the full updated row.

**DeleteTicket** -- `DELETE FROM tickets WHERE id = ?`

#### Postgres (`/home/chaschel/Documents/go/bchat/store/db/postgres/ticket.go` - 257 lines)

Same structure as SQLite but uses `$1, $2, ...` placeholders with manual `argCounter` tracking. Notable: has a bug/artifact on lines 57-59 where it initializes filters then immediately resets them (the SQLite code was copied and PG-specific placeholder logic was inserted after).

#### MySQL (`/home/chaschel/Documents/go/bchat/store/db/mysql/ticket.go` - 175 lines)

Older, simpler implementation. Does NOT include `type`, `tags`, or `tenant_id` columns. Uses `LastInsertId()` instead of `RETURNING`. Update does a follow-up `GetTicket` call to return the updated row instead of `RETURNING`.

**API Types:**

```go
type CreateTicketRequest struct {
    Title       string   `json:"title"`
    Description string   `json:"description"` // Must be "/m/..." memo link
    Status      string   `json:"status"`
    Priority    string   `json:"priority"`
    Type        string   `json:"type"`
    Tags        []string `json:"tags"`

}

type UpdateTicketRequest struct {

    Description *string  `json:"description"`
    Status      *string  `json:"status"`

    Type        *string  `json:"type"`
```
