}

type Ticket struct {
    ID          int32    `json:"id"`
    Title       string   `json:"title"`
    Description string   `json:"description"`
    Status      string   `json:"status"`
    Priority    string   `json:"priority"`
    CreatorID   int32    `json:"creatorId"`
    AssigneeID  *int32   `json:"assigneeId"`
    CreatedTs   int64    `json:"createdTs"`
    UpdatedTs   int64    `json:"updatedTs"`
    Type        string   `json:"type"`
    Tags        []string `json:"tags"`
}
```

**Handler Logic Summary:**

| Handler | Key Behavior |
|---------|-------------|
| **CreateTicket** | Sets tenant_id from context. Defaults: type=`TASK`, tags=`[]`. Validates `/m/...`. **Deduplication**: if description starts with `/m/`, checks for existing ticket with same (creator_id, description). If found, updates existing (smart merge of priority/type, superuser-only assignee change). |
| **ListTickets** | Applies tenant filter via `ApplyTicketTenantFilter()`. Non-superusers are forced to `CreatorID = userID` (can only see own tickets). Supports query params: `description`, `type`, `creatorId`. |
| **GetTicket** | Fetches by ID. **Smart fallback**: if not found by ID, tries to find memo with that ID and then finds ticket whose description is `/m/{memoUID}`. Enforces tenant ownership and creator-only access for non-superusers. |
| **UpdateTicket** | Verifies tenant ownership (superusers bypass). Non-superusers can only update own tickets and cannot change `assigneeId`. Only updatable fields specified in the request body are changed. |
| **DeleteTicket** | Superuser-only operation. Regular users cannot delete tickets (compliance requirement). |
| **ListTicketAssignees** | Superuser/internal-staff-only. Returns list of `{id, username}` for all users in the system (for assignee dropdown). |

### 6. TENANT ISOLATION

`ApplyTicketTenantFilter` in `/home/chaschel/Documents/go/bchat/server/router/api/v1/tenant_context.go` (lines 92-106):
- If the request context has a `tenantID`, sets `find.TenantID = tenantID`
- For scoped admins, derives `find.TenantIDs` slice from their `AllowedTenantIDs`

Security checks in handlers:
- Tenant ownership verified before update/get/delete
- Superuser bypass: `if tenantID != nil && ticket.TenantID != nil && *ticket.TenantID != *tenantID && !isSuperUser(user)`
- Non-superusers always filtered to own creator_id

### 8. HOW TICKETS CONNECT TO AGENT ESCALATIONS

In `/home/chaschel/Documents/go/bchat/server/router/api/v1/agent/service.go`:

**Ticket creation flow** for escalations:
1. `shouldCreateEscalationTicket()` -- checks if intent is "escalation" or `score.ShouldEscalate` is true
2. `handleExternalEscalation()` -- extracts customer info, checks for existing escalation ticket (dedup by sessionID), then calls `CreateEscalationTicket()`
3. `CreateEscalationTicket()` (line ~3890):
   - Generates ticket number via `GenerateTicketNumber()` (format: `TKT-YYYYMMDD-XXXX`)
   - Creates a **Memo** with Protected visibility and escalation details
   - Creates a **Ticket** with `Description: "/m/" + memoUID`, `Type: "agent_escalation"`, `TenantID` set
   - On memo creation failure, falls back to `createEscalationTicketFallback()` which puts all info inline in description
4. `findExistingEscalationTicket()` -- deduplicates by searching for `"agent_escalation"` type tickets with matching tenant and session marker in memo content
5. `systemTicketCreatorID()` -- resolves the system user (first user, fallback to creating "agent_system", fallback to user ID 1)

**Escalation types:**
- `"supervisor_request"` -- regular escalation
- `"complaint"` -- escalated with HIGH priority

**Tags:** The `"escalated"` tag is used by the frontend UI to show visual indicators.

## COMPLETE KNOWLEDGE BASE SYSTEM SUMMARY

### 1. DATA MODELS (`store/agent.go` — 1092 lines)

**Core entities** stored in the database after parsing:

| Entity | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `AgentTenant` | Tenant configuration (slug, company name, vertical, GUID, WidgetKey, processing options, allowed domains) |
| `AgentAudience` | Per-tenant audience config (audience_type = "external" or "internal", identity: role/tone/brand voice/guidelines, contact fields, thresholds, rate limiting) |
| `AgentSourceFile` | Raw uploaded file content (KB, policy, script) per tenant+audience, with versioning |
| `AgentTenantScript` | Conversation flow script (tenant-level, shared across audiences) |
| `AgentService` | Parsed from `<!-- @service -->` annotations in KB |
| `AgentExclusion` | Parsed from `<!-- @exclusion -->` annotations in KB |
| `AgentCoverage` | Parsed from `<!-- @coverage -->` annotations in KB |
| `AgentFAQ` | Parsed from `<!-- @faq -->` annotations in KB |
| `AgentSafetyProtocol` | Parsed from `<!-- @safety -->` annotations in KB |
| `AgentKBSection` | Parsed from `<!-- @section -->` annotations in KB |
| `AgentIntent` | Parsed from `<!-- @intent -->` annotations in POLICY |
| `AgentRule` | Parsed from `<!-- @rule -->` annotations in POLICY |
| `AgentKBMeta` | Parsed annotation metadata (type, value, key-value pairs) |
| `AgentSession` | Chat session state (phase, intent, urgency, coverage status, messages) |
| `AgentSessionObservation` | Observational memory entries |

### 2. PARSING (`parser.go` — 554 lines)

The `Parser` struct converts raw markdown into structured data:

**KB.MD annotations** (HTML comment format: `<!-- @type: value, key: value -->`):
- `@service: water_extraction, emergency: true` — Service entries with metadata (emergency flag, priority, etc.)
- `@faq: pricing` — FAQ entries
- `@exclusion` — Services NOT provided
- `@coverage` — Service coverage areas (postal codes)
- `@safety` — Safety protocols
- `@section` — Generic content sections

**POLICY.MD annotations**:
- `@identity` — Agent persona (role, tone, brand voice, guidelines)
- `@intent` — Customer intent categories (for intent routing/classification)
- `@rule` — Behavioral rules
- `@audience` — Audience-specific sections

**SCRIPT.MD** — Parsed into `ParsedScript` with stages (opening, triage, resolution, etc.) and multiline blocks per stage.

### 3. FILE UPLOAD & REINDEX FLOW (`handlers.go` — 1170 lines)

1. `HandleUploadAgentFile(c)` — POST handler accepting multipart upload for KB/policy/script
   - Parses content with `Parser.ParseKB()` or `ParsePolicy()` or `ParseScript()` depending on file type
   - Stores parsed entities via store methods (UpsertAgentService, UpsertAgentFAQ, etc.)
   - Also stores raw content in `AgentSourceFile`
2. `HandleRAGReindex(c)` — POST handler to rebuild RAG index
   - Loads KB content, chunks it, generates embeddings, inserts into LanceDB
3. Reindex also triggers on file upload (auto-reindex)

### 4. RAG PIPELINE (chunker → embedding → vector DB)

**`chunker.go`** (507 lines):
- `HeadingBasedChunker` with `ChunkByHeadings()` method
- Splits markdown by heading levels (H1, H2, H3)
- Each chunk = `DocumentChunk{ID, TenantID, AudienceType, ContentType, Title, Content, Code, IsEmergency, IsActive, Priority, SourceVersion, Embedding, IndexedAt}`
- Annotation metadata (e.g., `@service`, `@faq`) propagates to chunks as `IsEmergency`, `Priority`, `IsActive`

**`embedding.go`** (352 lines):
- `EmbeddingService` interface with `Embed(texts []string) ([][]float32, error)`
- Three providers via `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER` env var:
  - `openrouter` — calls OpenRouter embedding API (model: `text-embedding-3-small`, 1536 dims)
  - `local` — uses a local sentence-transformers model via subprocess (384 dims, MiniLM)
  - `mock` — returns random vectors (for testing, 1536 dims)
- Retry logic with configurable timeout (`EMBEDDING_TIMEOUT`)

**`vectordb.go`** (~630 lines):
- `VectorDB` interface: `Insert`, `Delete`, `Search`, `Close`
- `SearchQuery`: query text, tenant filter, audience type filter, top K, content types, hybrid search options
- `SearchResult`: chunk data + similarity score
- `NoOpVectorDB` — used when RAG is disabled
- `InMemoryVectorDB` — used when no LanceDB build tag
- `NewVectorDB` factory — selects implementation based on build tags + config

**`vectordb_lance.go`** (~790 lines, build tag `rag`):
- `LanceVectorDB` struct backed by LanceDB
- Features:
  - IVF-PQ index for approximate search
  - Hybrid search (vector 70% + BM25 30%) — configurable via `HYBRID_SEARCH_ENABLED` and `HybridWeights`
  - MMR diversification to avoid redundant results
  - Automatic migration from legacy table name
  - Checkpoint/commit management

### 5. SERVICE LAYER (`service.go` — 4659 lines)

**`LoadConfig(tenantSlug, audienceType) -> *AudienceConfig`** (lines 1374-1489):
- Checks config cache first
- Loads tenant → audience → all KB entities (services, exclusions, coverage, FAQs, safety, sections) → all POLICY entities (intents, rules) → script
- Loads learned behaviors from `LearningService`
- Loads raw KB/policy content (for phone extraction fallback)
- Determines `HasStructuredContent` flag (affects whether RAG-only or long-context fallback is used)

**`AudienceConfig` struct**:
```go
type AudienceConfig struct {
    TenantID, TenantSlug, CompanyName, AudienceType string
    Audience    *store.AgentAudience
    Services    []*store.AgentService
    Exclusions  []*store.AgentExclusion
    Coverage    []*store.AgentCoverage
    FAQs        []*store.AgentFAQ
    Safety      []*store.AgentSafetyProtocol
    Sections    []*store.AgentKBSection
    Intents     []*store.AgentIntent
    Rules       []*store.AgentRule
    Script      *store.AgentTenantScript
    LearnedBehaviors []*store.LearnedBehavior
    RawKB, RawPolicy string
    HasStructuredContent bool
}
```

**System prompt building** (two modes):
1. **Structured mode** (`buildSystemPrompt`): When `HasStructuredContent=true`, builds prompt with explicit sections:
   - Identity (role, tone, brand voice, guidelines)
   - Services (with emergency flag, priority)
   - FAQs (question → answer)
   - Exclusions (what the company does NOT do)
   - Safety protocols
   - Rules (behavioral constraints)
   - Intents (conversation routing)
   - Script stages (conversation flow)
2. **RAG mode** (`buildRAGSystemPrompt`): When content is unstructured or RAG is enabled, builds a leaner prompt and relies on `generateRAGResponse` to augment with retrieved chunks.

**Chat pipeline**:
- `ChatExternal` (lines 1572-1801): Anonymous users → session management, rate limiting, idempotency via `ClientMessageID`, HMAC session tokens for transcript access, bridge handoff support, then `processChat`
- `ChatInternal` (lines 1808-1871): Authenticated users → session persisted to DB, same `processChat` core logic

**`processChat`**: Core LLM interaction — builds system prompt + conversation history → calls OpenRouter API → handles streaming → runs Observer → returns response.

### 6. OBSERVATIONAL MEMORY (`observer.go` + `prompts/observer.txt` + `prompts/reflector.txt`)

- `prompts/observer.txt` (154 lines): Detailed instructions for extracting observations from conversations — user assertions vs. questions, temporal anchoring, priority emojis (🔴🟡🟢), XML output format (`<observations>`, `<current-task>`, `<suggested-response>`)

### KEY ARCHITECTURAL OBSERVATIONS

1. **Dual-mode architecture**: The system can work in two modes:
   - **Structured mode**: KB is parsed into structured DB entities → system prompt is built with explicit sections
   - **RAG mode**: KB content is chunked → embedded → stored in LanceDB → retrieved at query time

2. **Build-tag gating**: LanceDB integration is behind a `rag` build tag. Without it, `InMemoryVectorDB` is used (no persistence). This is critical for the build system.

3. **Audience isolation**: Each tenant can have multiple audiences (at minimum "external" and "internal"), each with its own identity, KB content, policies, and RAG index. `AudienceType` is a first-class filter throughout the pipeline.

4. **Annotation system is extensible**: The `ResolveAnnotation` helper and `AgentKBMeta` type support arbitrary key-value metadata on annotations, making it easy to add new annotation types without code changes.

5. **Idempotency layer**: `ClientMessageID` + `AgentMessageRecord` table enables exactly-once delivery even across process restarts.

6. **Bridge handoff**: The system supports human handoff with operator assignment, queueing, and real-time messaging integration.

## Complete File Inventory and Analysis

### 1. Observational Memory (OM) - `observer.go`
**File:** `/home/chaschel/Documents/go/bchat/server/router/api/v1/agent/observer.go` (563 lines)

**Core Architecture:**
- The `RunObserver` method is the main pipeline method triggered asynchronously after each chat message exchange.
- Two LLM prompt templates are embedded at compile time via `//go:embed`:
  - `prompts/observer.txt` - The observer system prompt
  - `prompts/reflector.txt` - The reflector (compression) system prompt
- **Trivial message filtering** uses a regex compiled at `init()` to skip messages matching patterns like "ok", "thanks", "yes", "no", "lol", etc.
- **Pipeline steps:**
  1. Retrieve session (from in-memory cache first, fallback to store)
  2. Retrieve existing observations (supports both `thread` scope by `sessionID` and `resource` scope by `resourceID` for cross-conversation memory)
  3. Determine unobserved messages since `LastObservedMsgIndex`
  4. Filter trivial messages
  5. Call Observer LLM with retry logic (`withRetry`)
  6. Parse XML-tagged output (`<observations>`, `<current-task>`, `<suggested-response>`)
  7. Merge new observations with existing log
  8. Check token count against `TokenThreshold`; if exceeded, trigger Reflector for compression
  9. Persist the updated observation log via `UpsertObservationLog`
  10. Optionally index observations to RAG (Hybrid OM + RAG) if `HybridEnabled && HybridIndexObservations`

**Key Helper Functions:**
- `parseXMLTag(content, tagName)` - Extracts content between XML tags using regex `(?is)<tagName>(.*?)</tagName>`
- `estimateTokens(text)` - Approximate token count (len/4)
- `withRetry(ctx, maxAttempts, delayMs, fn)` - Retry with backoff
- `isRetryable(err)` - Retries on all errors except context cancellation/deadline
- `filterTrivialMessages(messages)` - Filters out trivial/acknowledgment messages
- `storeObservationFromBuffer()` - Stores pre-computed buffered observations

### 2. OM Buffer - `observer_buffer.go`
**File:** `/home/chaschel/Documents/go/bchat/server/router/api/v1/agent/observer_buffer.go` (318 lines)

**Architecture:**
- `ObserverBuffer` manages background pre-computation of observations to reduce latency
- Contains a `map[memorySessionKey]*BufferState` of per-session buffers
- Uses a buffered channel (`triggerChan`) for async triggers
- Background workers: `bufferWorker()` and `cleanupWorker()` (5-minute ticker, 30-min buffer expiration)

**Buffer States:**
- `BufferState` holds: `PendingObservations`, `PendingCurrentTask`, `PendingSuggestedResp`, `TokenCount`, `LastBufferTime`, `LastBufferedMsgIndex`, `ResourceID`, `IsActive`

**Threshold-based Activation:**
- `ShouldTriggerBuffer(unobservedTokens, threshold)` - triggers at `BufferTokens` fraction (default 20% of threshold)
- `ShouldActivateBuffer(unobservedTokens, threshold)` - activates when threshold reached
- `ShouldBlock(unobservedTokens, threshold)` - forces synchronous observation at `BlockAfter` fraction (default 120%)
- `BufferTokens`, `BufferActivation`, `BlockAfter` are configurable fractions of `ObserverTokenThreshold`

**Key Methods:**
- `TriggerBuffer(tenantID, sessionID)` - Schedules background observation
- `GetAndActivateBuffer()` - Returns buffered observations and marks as activated (lock-protected)
- `ClearBuffer()` - Removes buffer after activation
- `HasBuffer()` - Checks for pending buffer
- `runBufferObservation()` - Performs actual LLM observation in background

| `ObserverTokenThreshold` | `OM_OBSERVER_TOKEN_THRESHOLD` | 30000 (observer trigger) |
| `RetryAttempts` | `OM_RETRY_ATTEMPTS` | 3 |
| `RetryDelayMs` | `OM_RETRY_DELAY_MS` | 1000 |
| `BufferTokens` | `OM_BUFFER_TOKENS` | 0.2 (20%) |
| `BufferActivation` | `OM_BUFFER_ACTIVATION` | 0.8 (80%) |
| `BlockAfter` | `OM_BLOCK_AFTER` | 1.2 (120%) |
| `Scope` | `OM_SCOPE` | "thread" |

**Scopes:**

- `OMScopeResource` ("resource") - Observations shared across all sessions for a user

Humans are backup for edge cases.** Every architectural decision flows from this:\n\n- The KB is machine-readable (annotations), not just human-readable markdown\n- Every conversation is a data point for analysis and improvement\n- Tickets are created only when escalation is needed — and they carry the full conversation context\n- The customer never needs to know a ticket number exists\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 2: The bchat Thesis\n\nThe bchat approach to customer support can be summarized in four principles:\n\n#### Principle 1: Conversation Is the Record\n\nIn Intercom + Jira, the ticket is the record and the conversation is ephemeral. In bchat, **the conversation is the record** and tickets are annotations on conversations.\n\n```go\n// The chat session contains everything:\ntype AgentSession struct {\n    // ... standard session fields\n    \n    // Conversation history — the full record\n    messages TEXT DEFAULT '[]'  // JSON array of all messages\n    \n    // Derived state\n    phase             string   // \"triage\", \"resolution\", \"completed\"\n    current_intent    string   // detected intent from policy\n    urgency_level     int      // computed urgency\n    detected_service  string   // matched service from KB\n    \n    // Escalation marker\n    is_completed      bool\n    completion_reason string   // \"resolved\", \"escalated\", \"abandoned\"\n}\n```\n\nWhen an escalation happens, the ticket is created by copying the conversation context into a memo linked to the ticket:\n\n```go\n// In service.go (simplified):\nfunc (s *Service) CreateEscalationTicket(ctx context.Context, session *AgentSession, reason string) (*store.Ticket, error) {\n    // 1. Create a memo with the full conversation context\n    memo := s.store.CreateMemo(ctx, &store.Memo{\n        Content:   formatEscalationContext(session, reason),\n        Visibility: \"PROTECTED\",  // only internal agents\n    })\n    \n    // 2. Create a ticket linked to the memo\n    ticket := s.store.CreateTicket(ctx, &store.Ticket{\n        Type:        \"agent_escalation\",\n        Description: \"/m/\" + memo.UID,\n        Status:      \"OPEN\",\n        Priority:    \"HIGH\",\n        Tags:        []string{\"escalated\"},\n    })\n    return ticket, nil\n}\n```\n\nThe customer never sees \"TKT-45921.\" They see their ongoing conversation, now handled by a human who has full context.\n\n#### Principle 2: Resolve Before Escalating\n\nThe default path is **AI resolution**. Escalation is a specific, measured decision based on:\n\n- **Intent detection**: Is the customer's intent in the KB? If not, escalate.\n- **Confidence threshold**: Is the AI confident in its response? Below 0.85, consider escalation.\n- **Urgency/emergency**: Safety-related queries always go to a human.\n- **Customer persistence**: If the customer asks the same question three times despite correct answers, escalate.\n\n```go\n// In service.go (simplified escalation decision):\nfunc (s *Service) shouldEscalate(score *store.EscalationScore) bool {\n    return score.ShouldEscalate ||\n        score.Confidence < 0.85 ||\n        score.Urgency > 7\n}\n```\n\n#### Principle 3: Close the Loop\n\nEvery conversation generates data:\n- **Observation log**: What was discussed, what the customer wanted, what was resolved\n- **Analysis scores**: How well the AI performed (intent recognition, service alignment, policy compliance, etc.)\n- **Learning memory**: Common issues, improvement areas, pending suggestions\n\nThis data feeds back into the KB. If customers keep asking about a service not in the KB, that's a signal to add it.\n\n#### Principle 4: The Customer's Experience Is the Only Metric\n\nNot ticket volume, not first-response time, not SLA compliance. The metrics that matter:\n\n| Metric | What It Measures | bchat Equivalent |\n|--------|-----------------|------------------|\n| Resolution rate | % of conversations resolved without escalation | `completion_reason = 'resolved'` |\n| Time to resolve | How long to answer the customer's question | Message count + LLM latency |\n| Customer effort | How hard did the customer have to work? | Message count (fewer = better), rephrasing rate |\n| Follow-through | Did the customer act on the AI's advice? | Lead conversion rate |\n| Sentiment | Was the customer satisfied? | Analysis sentiment category |\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 3: A Day in the Life\n\nLet's walk through three scenarios to see how bchat works in practice. Each scenario reveals a different architectural capability.\n\n#### Scenario A: External Customer — Plumbing Emergency\n\nA homeowner named Sarah has a burst pipe at 2 AM. She visits the website of \"Apex Restoration\" (a bchat tenant) and clicks the chat widget.\n\n**What happens on the backend:**\n\n1. A POST to `/api/v1/agent/apex-restoration/chat` creates a new session with `audience_type = 'external'`\n2. The system loads Apex's AudienceConfig for the `external` audience: KB services, policies, and script\n3. Sarah types \"I have water pouring from my ceiling\"\n\n**Intent detection** (from policy):\n\n```\nThe LLM classifies: intent = \"water_extraction\", emergency = true\n```\n\n**KB response** (from structured content):\n\n```\nSystem prompt builds:\n  Role: Customer Service Representative\n  Tone: Professional, empathetic\n  Service: Water Extraction — 24/7 emergency response\n  Emergency phone: (555) 123-4567\n  Script Stage: Opening → Greet the customer → Ask how you can help\n```\n\n**AI response:** \"I'm sorry to hear about the burst pipe, Sarah. This is an emergency situation. Our water extraction team is available 24/7. Would you like me to send someone right away?\"\n\n4. Sarah confirms. The AI captures her contact info.\n5. After the conversation, the system checks `shouldEscalate`:\n   - Intent matched ✓\n   - Service found ✓\n   - No escalation needed\n6. **Lead captured:** Sarah's info is stored as a lead for follow-up.\n\n**Sarah's experience:** She got immediate help at 2 AM, didn't wait for a human, didn't open a ticket, didn't repeat herself. She'll get a follow-up email tomorrow asking if everything was resolved.\n\n**No ticket was created.** The conversation is the record.\n\n#### Scenario B: Escalation to Human Agent\n\nA customer named James is talking to the AI about a complex insurance claim. The AI detects the intent but the customer is not satisfied.\n\n**Escalation path:**\n\n1. `shouldEscalate()` returns true (customer has asked \"Can I speak to a human?\" three times)\n2. `CreateEscalationTicket()` generates:\n   - A memo with the full conversation transcript\n   - A ticket with `type = \"agent_escalation\"`, `priority = \"HIGH\"`, `tags = [\"escalated\"]`\n3. The ticket appears on the internal Kanban board at `/tickets`\n4. An agent picks up the ticket, sees the full conversation context in the linked memo\n5. The customer is told \"I've connected you with a specialist who has all the details of your situation\"\n\n**James's experience:** He never saw a ticket number. He never repeated himself. The human agent knew everything.\n\n#### Scenario C: Internal Agent — Managing Support Queue\n\nAn internal support agent logs into bchat as an authenticated user. They see:\n\n- `/tickets` — Kanban board with OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, CLOSED columns\n- Each card shows: title, priority chip (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH), type chip (TASK/agent_escalation), escalation badge, assignee avatar\n- Escalated tickets are at the top with red badges\n- Clicking a ticket opens a side panel with full context from the memo\n\n**Agent actions:**\n- Drag from OPEN to IN_PROGRESS to self-assign\n- Reply in the conversation (memo comments)\n- Drag to CLOSED when resolved\n- View analytics: resolution rate, escalation rate, common intents\n\n**The agent's tool is not Jira.** It's a conversational interface augmented by Kanban for triage. The ticket exists only for the agent's workflow — the customer never interacts with it.\n\n---\n\n## Part 2: The Dual-Audience System — Internal vs External\n\n### Chapter 4: The Audience Model\n\nbchat's audience model is the key architectural insight that enables replacing both Intercom and Jira with one system.\n\n#### One Tenant, Two Audiences\n\nEvery tenant has at least two audiences:\n\n| Audience | Users | Auth | Chat Endpoint | Features |\n|----------|-------|------|---------------|----------|\n| `external` | Anonymous website visitors | Widget embed + HMAC token | `POST /api/v1/agent/:slug/chat` | AI-only, lead capture, optional bridge handoff |\n| `internal` | Authenticated staff | JWT with role | `POST /api/v1/agent/:slug/chat/internal` | AI + human, full ticket system, Kanban, analytics |\n\n#### Audience Configuration\n\nEach audience has its own configuration in `agent_audiences`:\n\n```go\ntype AgentAudience struct {\n    ID        int32\n    TenantID  int32\n    AudienceType string // \"external\" | \"internal\"\n    \n    // Identity\n    Role    string // e.g., \"Customer Service Representative\"\n    Tone    string // \"Professional, empathetic\"\n    BrandVoice string\n    Guidelines string\n    \n    // Contact\n    EmergencyPhone string\n    SecondaryPhones []string\n    \n    // Behavior\n    RateLimitRPM              int  // external: 60, internal: 120\n    RequireContactOnFallback  bool // external: true (capture email before handoff)\n    MaxMessageLength          int  // external: 2000, internal: 4000\n    EmergencyUrgencyThreshold int  // 4 = >50% threshold for human involvement\n    EscalationConfidenceThreshold float64 // 0.85\n}\n```\n\n**The same tenant can have dramatically different configs for each audience:**\n\n```markdown\n<!-- For external customers: helpful, concise, empathetic -->\n@identity\n- Role: Customer Service Representative\n- Tone: Warm and professional\n- Guidelines: Never ask for payment info in chat. Always offer to schedule a callback.\n\n<!-- For internal agents: tactical, precise, data-rich -->\n@identity\n- Role: Support Operations Analyst\n- Tone: Clear and actionable\n- Guidelines: Always include ticket reference. Verify SLA compliance before committing.\n```\n\n#### Why Audiences Matter for CX\n\nThe audience system enables three critical CX capabilities:\n\n1. **Different KB for different audiences.** External customers see service descriptions and FAQs. Internal agents see escalation procedures and compliance rules — in the same KB.MD file, just in different audience sections.\n\n2. **Different escalation paths.** External customers escalate to a ticket (invisible to them). Internal agents escalate to a supervisor with full context.\n\n3. **Different rate limits.** External users are limited to 60 RPM per IP. Internal agents get 120 RPM because they need to test and iterate.\n\n#### The KB.MD Audience Section\n\nIn the KB.MD file, you can mark content for specific audiences:\n\n```markdown\n<!-- @audience: external -->\n\n<!-- @service: water_extraction, emergency: true -->\n## Water Extraction\n24/7 emergency response for standing water removal...\n\nWe serve all of Cook County within 2 hours.\n\n<!-- @faq: pricing -->\n## How much does it cost?\nCosts vary based on extent of damage. We provide free estimates.\n\n---\n\n<!-- @audience: internal -->\n\n<!-- @service: water_extraction -->\n## Water Extraction — Internal Protocol\n### Escalation Criteria\n- If moisture detected in walls → dispatch structural team\n- If sewage involved → dispatch biohazard team\n- If customer has filed insurance claim → route to claims department\n```\n\nWhen the system loads config for `audience_type = 'external'`, it only loads the external sections. When loading for `audience_type = 'internal'`, it loads the internal sections. This is enforced at the database query level via `ListAgentServices(find.FindAgentService{TenantID: tenantID, AudienceType: \"external\"})`.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 5: The External Customer Flow\n\nThe external customer flow is the primary experience. This is where bchat replaces Intercom.\n\n#### Entry Points\n\nExternal customers can start a conversation from:\n\n- **Embedded widget**: A JavaScript widget on the tenant's website (via `widget_key` and `guid`)\n- **Direct API**: `POST /api/v1/agent/:slug/chat` with minimal parameters\n- **Bridge channel**: External messaging platforms (Twilio, WhatsApp, Messenger) via the bridge delivery system\n\n#### Session Lifecycle\n\n```\n1. Customer opens widget → POST /chat\n   ├── Tenant resolved by slug\n   ├── Audience set to \"external\"\n   ├── Session created (in-memory or DB)\n   └── HMAC session token generated for transcript access\n\n2. Customer sends message → POST /chat with session_id\n   ├── Rate limit check (60 RPM per IP)\n   ├── Idempotency check (ClientMessageID)\n   ├── Intent detection (LLM classifies against policy intents)\n   ├── KB lookup (structured content or RAG retrieval)\n   ├── LLM response generation\n   ├── Observer triggers (async)\n   │   ├── Check token threshold for buffer\n   │   ├── Run Observer LLM\n   │   ├── Update observation log\n   │   └── Check reflector threshold (compress if needed)\n   └── Response streamed back to widget\n\n3. Customer satisfied → chat ends\n   ├── completion_reason = \"resolved\"\n   ├── Lead captured (if contact info provided)\n   └── Session stored for analysis\n\n4. Customer not satisfied → escalation\n   ├── shouldEscalate() = true\n   ├── Escalation ticket created (invisible to customer)\n   ├── Bridge handoff queued (if bridge enabled)\n   └── Customer notified: \"A specialist will join shortly\"\n```\n\n#### The No-Account Promise\n\nExternal customers never need an account. The session is identified by a session ID generated server-side and returned in the chat response. The HMAC token allows the customer to view their transcript later without authentication:\n\n```go\n// In service.go — external chat handler\nfunc (s *Service) ChatExternal(ctx context.Context, req *ChatRequest) (*ChatResponse, error) {\n    // ...\n    session, err := s.store.CreateAgentSession(ctx, &store.AgentSession{\n        TenantID:     tenantID,\n        AudienceType: \"external\",\n        Phase:        \"triage\",\n    })\n    \n    // HMAC session token for transcript access\n    sessionToken := generateSessionToken(session.ID, tenant.Key)\n    \n    return &ChatResponse{\n        SessionID:    session.ID,\n        SessionToken: sessionToken,\n        Message:      response,\n    }, nil\n}\n```\n\nThis is critical for CX: **zero friction to start a conversation.** No signup, no ticket creation, no \"before we begin\" form.\n\n#### Rate Limiting with Grace\n\nExternal rate limiting in bchat uses a per-IP, per-tenant sliding window:\n\n```go\n// Current behavior (simplified):\nfunc (s *Service) checkRateLimit(ctx context.Context, tenantID int32, clientIP string) (bool, error) {\n    allowed, err := s.store.CheckAndIncrementAgentRateLimit(ctx, tenantID, \"external\", clientIP, 60)\n    if !allowed {\n        // Return a friendly message, not a 429\n        return false, fmt.Errorf(\"I'm receiving a lot of requests right now. Please wait a moment and try again.\")\n    }\n    return true, nil\n}\n```\n\nThe rate limit response is designed to be customer-friendly — not a cryptic HTTP status code but a human-readable message from the AI. This is a deliberate CX choice: the customer should never see an error page from the chat widget.\n\n#### Idempotency for Safe Retry\n\nExternal customers on unreliable connections (mobile, public WiFi) may send the same message twice. The `ClientMessageID` field ensures exactly-once processing:\n\n```go\ntype ChatRequest struct {\n    SessionID       string `json:\"sessionId\"`\n    Message         string `json:\"message\"`\n    ClientMessageID string `json:\"clientMessageId\"`  // Idempotency key\n    \n    // If the same ClientMessageID is sent twice,\n    // the second call returns the cached response.\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 6: The Internal Agent Flow\n\nInternal agents (support staff, admins, supervisors) have a different experience designed for productivity.\n\n#### Entry Points\n\nInternal agents access bchat via:\n\n- **Web UI**: Full dashboard at `/` with Kanban board, analytics, and configuration\n- **Internal chat API**: `POST /api/v1/agent/:slug/chat/internal` (authenticated)\n- **Memo system**: Full memo (note-taking app) for documentation\n\n#### The Kanban Board\n\nThe ticket Kanban at `/tickets` is the internal agent's primary tool. However, it is deliberately **not Jira**:\n\n| Jira | bchat Kanban | Why |\n|------|-------------|-----|\n| Required fields on create | Minimal required: title only | Reduce friction |\n| Custom workflows per project | Three columns: OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, CLOSED | Simplicity |\n| Status transitions with permissions | Drag and drop | Intuitive |\n| Email notifications | Real-time SSE notifications | Immediate |\n| Customer portal | No customer portal | Tickets are internal |\n\nThe Kanban board uses `@dnd-kit` for drag-and-drop:\n\n```typescript\n// In TicketKanban.tsx\nconst columns = [\n    { id: 'OPEN', title: 'Open', tickets: openTickets },\n    { id: 'IN_PROGRESS', title: 'In Progress', tickets: inProgressTickets },\n    { id: 'CLOSED', title: 'Closed', tickets: closedTickets },\n];\n\n// Dragging to a different column calls:\nconst handleStatusChange = (ticketId: number, newStatus: string) => {\n    updateTicket({ id: ticketId, status: newStatus });\n};\n```\n\n#### The Escalation View\n\nThe escalation view is a filtered Kanban showing only `agent_escalation` type tickets:\n\n```go\n// In ticket_service.go\nfunc (s *Service) ListTicketAssignees(c echo.Context) error {\n    // Superuser / admin only\n    // Returns list of users for assignee dropdown\n}\n```\n\nAgents see escalated tickets with:\n- **Title**: \"Escalation from [Customer Name]\"\n- **Priority**: HIGH (auto-set by escalation logic)\n- **Type badge**: \"Escalation\" (red)\n- **Tags**: \"escalated\" (shown as a badge in the UI)\n- **Memo link**: Click to open the full conversation context\n\n#### Analytics for Internal Agents\n\nInternal agents have access to analytics (via the analysis system):\n\n- **Resolution rate**: % of conversations resolved without escalation\n- **Average messages per conversation**: Indicator of efficiency (fewer = better)\n- **Common intents**: What customers are asking about most\n- **Lead conversion rate**: How many leads turned into actual business\n- **Sentiment trend**: Is customer satisfaction improving or declining?\n\nThese analytics are generated from `AgentAnalysisResult` records:\n\n```go\ntype AgentAnalysisResult struct {\n    ID               string\n    TenantID         int32\n    ConversationID   string\n    ConversationType string // \"simulation\" or \"chat\"\n    UserID           int32\n    Score            int    // 0-100\n    Grade            string // \"A\", \"B\", \"C\", \"D\", \"F\"\n    Breakdown        AnalysisBreakdown  // 6 categories\n    Issues           []AnalysisIssue\n    Suggestions      []string\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n## Part 3: Knowledge Management — The Heart of AI Support\n\n### Chapter 7: KB.MD — The Single Source of Truth\n\nThe Knowledge Base is the most important file in the system. It determines everything the AI knows, every service it can offer, and every answer it can give.\n\n#### Structure\n\nA well-written KB.MD has three principles:\n\n1. **Annotate everything.** Every service, FAQ, exclusion, and section should have a `@type` annotation.\n2. **Write for the AI, not just for humans.** The AI reads the raw content. Use clear, unambiguous language. Avoid marketing fluff.\n3. **Think in terms of intents.** What is the customer trying to do? Map content to those intents.\n\n```markdown\n# Apex Restoration Services\n\n<!-- @audience: external -->\n\n<!-- @service: water_extraction, emergency: true, priority: 1 -->\n## Water Extraction\nWe provide 24/7 emergency water extraction services.\n\n- **Response time:** Within 2 hours for all of Cook County\n- **Equipment:** Industrial-grade vacuums, air movers, dehumidifiers\n- **Process:** Assessment → Extraction → Drying → Sanitization → Restoration\n\n**What to do while waiting:**\n1. Turn off water at the main valve if safe\n2. Move valuables to dry area\n3. Do NOT use electrical appliances near standing water\n\n<!-- @faq: water_damage_insurance -->\n## Does insurance cover water damage?\nMost homeowner's insurance policies cover sudden and accidental water damage...\n```\n\n#### Why Annotations Matter for CX\n\nAnnotations are not metadata — they are **behavior directives**:\n\n- `emergency: true` — The AI will prioritize this service and use urgent language\n- `priority: 1` — This service appears first in the system prompt\n- `@faq: pricing` — The AI knows this is a FAQ, not a service offering, and will answer differently\n\nWithout annotations, the AI treats everything equally. With annotations, the AI understands the **intent and importance** of each piece of content.\n\n#### What Happens When KB Is Missing\n\nIf a customer asks about a service not in the KB, three things happen:\n\n1. **Intent detection fails** — the AI does not recognize the intent\n2. **Service matching fails** — no service is found in structured content or RAG\n3. **Fallback behavior** — the AI either:\n   - Says \"I don't have information about that\" (safe but unhelpful)\n   - Guesses (dangerous — hallucination risk)\n   - Escalates to a human (best for CX)\n\nThe best KB is one that covers every service the tenant offers. The analysis system tracks \"coverage gaps\" as `CommonIssues`:\n\n```go\ntype CommonIssue struct {\n    Category    string // \"coverage_gap\"\n    Description string // \"Customer asked about mold remediation, not in KB\"\n    Occurrences int\n    LastSeen    string\n}\n```\n\nThis feeds into the learning memory, alerting the tenant admin to add missing content.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 8: POLICY.MD — The Agent's Constitution\n\nWhile the KB defines **what** the AI knows, the policy defines **how** the AI behaves.\n\n#### Policy Structure\n\n```markdown\n<!-- @audience: external -->\n\n<!-- @identity -->\n- Role: Customer Service Representative\n- Tone: Warm, professional, empathetic\n- Brand Voice: We are experts but not condescending. We educate without overwhelming.\n- Guidelines:\n  - Never make promises about pricing without a supervisor\n  - Always ask for permission before scheduling a visit\n  - If the customer is angry, acknowledge their frustration first\n\n<!-- @intent: schedule_service -->\n## Schedule Service\nCustomer wants to book an appointment for a specific service.\n\nSteps:\n1. Confirm the service they need\n2. Check coverage area (see Coverage section)\n3. Offer available time slots\n4. Collect contact information\n5. Confirm the appointment\n\n<!-- @intent: emergency -->\n## Emergency\nCustomer has an urgent situation requiring immediate response.\n\nSteps:\n1. Confirm safety (are they in immediate danger?)\n2. If yes: instruct them to call 911, then contact emergency dispatch\n3. If no: provide emergency phone number\n4. Dispatch emergency team\n5. Follow up within 1 hour\n\n<!-- @rule: no_pricing_over_chat -->\n## Pricing Rule\nNever provide exact pricing over chat. Always say \"pricing varies based on the specific situation\" and offer a free estimate.\n```\n\n#### How Policy Drives Behavior\n\nThe policy is not a static document. It is parsed into structured data:\n\n```go\ntype AgentIntent struct {\n    Code        string // \"schedule_service\"\n    Name        string // \"Schedule Service\"\n    Category    string // \"booking\"\n    Description string // \"Customer wants to book...\"\n    Action      string // \"schedule\"\n    Urgency     int    // 5\n    // ...\n}\n\ntype AgentRule struct {\n    Code        string // \"no_pricing_over_chat\"\n    Name        string // \"Pricing Rule\"\n    Description string // \"Never provide exact pricing...\"\n    Priority    int    // 10 (higher = more important)\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\nThese are injected into the system prompt as structured sections:\n\n```\n=== IDENTITY ===\nRole: Customer Service Representative\nTone: Warm, professional, empathetic\n...\n\n=== INTENTS ===\nWhen a customer wants to schedule a service:\n  1. Confirm the service they need\n  2. Check coverage area\n  ...\n\n=== RULES ===\n- Never provide exact pricing over chat.\n- Always ask for permission before scheduling.\n```\n\n**The AI does not have to learn the policy.** The policy is literally in the prompt. This is why bchat works without fine-tuning — the behavioral rules are context, not weights.\n\n#### Why Policy Matters for CX\n\nA good policy prevents the most common AI support failures:\n\n| Failure | Cause | Policy Solution |\n|---------|-------|----------------|\n| AI invents pricing | No pricing rule | `@rule: no_pricing_over_chat` |\n| AI is rude after customer is angry | No tone guidelines | \"Acknowledge frustration first\" |\n| AI schedules without permission | No permission rule | \"Always ask before scheduling\" |\n| AI escalates unnecessarily | No escalation criteria | Confidence threshold + intent matching |\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 9: SCRIPT.MD — Conversation Architecture\n\nThe script defines the conversation flow. It is the closest thing to a \"playbook\" for the AI.\n\n#### Script Structure\n\n```markdown\n<!-- @audience: external -->\n\n## Stage: Opening\n- Greet the customer warmly\n- Introduce yourself and the company\n- Ask how you can help today\n\n## Stage: Triage\n- Ask clarifying questions to identify the issue\n- Match to a service or FAQ from the knowledge base\n- If urgent (emergency), skip to Emergency Protocol\n- If unclear, ask: \"Can you tell me more about what's happening?\"\n\n## Stage: Resolution\n- Provide solution based on KB\n- Confirm the customer is satisfied\n- Offer next steps (schedule service, send info, etc.)\n\n## Stage: Closing\n- Thank the customer\n- Ask if there's anything else you can help with\n- Let them know they'll receive a follow-up email\n```\n\n#### How Script Becomes Behavior\n\nThe script is parsed into stages:\n\n```go\ntype ParsedScript struct {\n    TenantID  int32\n    AudienceType string\n    Stages    []ScriptStage\n}\n\ntype ScriptStage struct {\n    Name    string // \"Opening\"\n    Content string  // \"- Greet the customer...\\n- Ask how you can help...\"\n    Index   int\n}\n```\n\nThe LLM prompt includes the script and a state machine instruction:\n\n```\n=== CONVERSATION SCRIPT ===\n\nCurrent stage: Opening\n\nStage: Opening\n- Greet the customer warmly\n- Introduce yourself\n- Ask how you can help\n\nStage: Triage\n...\n\nYou are currently in the \"Opening\" stage. Follow the script for this stage.\nWhen the customer's need is clear, transition to \"Triage\".\n```\n\nThe AI is instructed to progress through stages naturally. The script is a guide, not a straitjacket — the AI can skip stages if the customer's intent is immediately clear.\n\n#### Script for Internal Agents\n\nInternal agents have a different script focused on efficiency:\n\n```markdown\n<!-- @audience: internal -->\n\n## Stage: Review\n- Review the escalation memo for full context\n- Verify all customer information is collected\n- Check for any previous interactions (via observation log)\n\n## Stage: Resolution\n- Address the specific escalation reason\n- If the AI missed something, correct it in the memo notes\n- Update the ticket status to IN_PROGRESS\n\n## Stage: Closing\n- Confirm resolution with the customer\n- Set ticket to CLOSED\n- Add summary note to the escalation memo for AI training\n```\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 10: RAG vs Structured Mode\n\nNot all KB content is well-structured. Some tenants have long documents, policy PDFs, or technical manuals. bchat supports two modes for handling KB content.\n\n#### Structured Mode\n\nWhen the KB is well-structured (services, FAQs, exclusions, etc. are annotated), the system builds a **structured system prompt**:\n\n```\n=== SERVICES ===\n- Water Extraction (24/7 emergency, priority: 1)\n- Mold Remediation (business hours, priority: 3)\n\n=== FAQS ===\n- Pricing: Costs vary based on extent of damage.\n\n=== EXCLUSIONS ===\nWe do NOT provide: sewage cleanup, pest control.\n```\n\n**Pros:** Precise, controllable, no retrieval errors.\n**Cons:** Requires well-annotated KB, limited to what fits in the context window.\n\n#### RAG Mode\n\nWhen the KB is unstructured or very large, the system uses **Retrieval-Augmented Generation**:\n\n```\n1. Chunk KB into segments (~500 tokens each)\n2. Embed each chunk via OpenRouter text-embedding-3-small\n3. Store embeddings in LanceDB\n4. At query time, retrieve top-K chunks similar to the query\n5. Inject retrieved chunks into the prompt\n```\n\nThe `HeadingBasedChunker` in `chunker.go` splits by markdown headings:\n\n```go\ntype DocumentChunk struct {\n    ID            string\n    TenantID      int32\n    AudienceType  string\n    ContentType   string // \"service\", \"faq\", \"general\"\n    Title         string // heading text\n    Content       string // chunk content\n    Code          string // annotation code (e.g., \"water_extraction\")\n    IsEmergency   bool\n    Priority      int\n    IsActive      bool\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\n#### Hybrid Mode\n\nYou can use both: structured content for the core system prompt and RAG for supplementary retrieval:\n\n```\nSystem prompt: Identity + Rules + Intents (always in context)\nRAG context: Retrieved chunks for specific queries (on-demand)\n```\n\nThis is the recommended approach for production. The structured content defines the AI's behavior; RAG provides the AI's knowledge.\n\n#### CX Implications\n\n| Mode | Best For | CX Risk |\n|------|----------|---------|\n| Structured | Simple service catalogs (< 20 services) | KB maintenance burden |\n| RAG | Large knowledge bases (manuals, policies) | Retrieval failures, latency |\n| Hybrid | Most production scenarios | Configuration complexity |\n\n**The CX golden rule of RAG:** A bad retrieval is worse than no retrieval. If the RAG system returns an irrelevant chunk, the AI will hallucinate around it. Always test RAG recall before deploying to production.\n\n---\n\n## Part 4: Observational Memory & Agent Learning\n\n### Chapter 11: How Observational Memory Works\n\nObservational Memory (OM) is bchat's solution to conversational amnesia — the problem where the AI forgets what was discussed in previous exchanges.\n\n#### The Problem It Solves\n\nWithout OM, the AI's memory is limited to the conversation history in the current session's context window. But context windows are finite (typically 8K–128K tokens), and important information can fall out:\n\n- Customer preferences (\"I always call on Tuesdays\")\n- Previous issues (\"I had a leak last month too\")\n- Unresolved concerns (\"You didn't answer my question about pricing\")\n\nOM solves this by **compressing conversation history into a structured observation log** that persists beyond the context window.\n\n#### The Pipeline\n\nOM works in three stages:\n\n**Stage 1: Buffer (low-cost pre-computation)**\n\nAfter each chat response, the system checks if the unobserved tokens exceed the buffer threshold (20% of `ObserverTokenThreshold`). If so, it triggers an async buffer observation:\n\n```go\n// In service.go (after chat response)\nfunc (s *Service) triggerObservation(ctx context.Context, session *store.AgentSession) {\n    shouldBuffer := unobservedTokens >= int(float64(config.ObserverTokenThreshold)*config.BufferTokens)\n    shouldBlock := unobservedTokens >= int(float64(config.ObserverTokenThreshold)*config.BlockAfter)\n    \n    if shouldBlock {\n        // Synchronous — block the response until observation is done\n        s.RunObserver(ctx, session)\n    } else if shouldBuffer {\n        // Async — pre-compute in background\n        s.ObserverBuffer.TriggerBuffer(session.TenantID, session.ID)\n    }\n}\n```\n\n**Stage 2: Observer (extract structured observations)**\n\nWhen the token threshold (default 30,000) is reached, the Observer LLM is called with the conversation transcript. It extracts:\n\n```xml\n<observations>\n🔴 Customer is frustrated about delayed response times.\n🟡 Customer mentioned they have a basement renovation planned.\n🟢 Customer preferred email contact over phone.\n</observations>\n<current-task>Resolve complaint about response time and schedule follow-up.</current-task>\n<suggested-response>Apologize for the delay, explain the standard response time, offer a timeline for resolution.</suggested-response>\n```\n\nThe observer prompt (`prompts/observer.txt`, 154 lines) instructs the LLM to:\n- Distinguish user assertions from questions (🔴🟡🟢 priority)\n- Preserve unusual phrasing and precise action verbs\n- Use temporal anchoring (\"Customer reported X on Tuesday\")\n- Output in XML for reliable parsing\n\n**Stage 3: Reflector (compress when too large)**\n\nWhen the observation log exceeds the token threshold (default 2,000), the Reflector compresses it:\n\n```go\n// In observer.go\nfunc (s *Service) RunReflector(ctx context.Context, session *store.AgentSession) error {\n    tokensInLog := estimateTokens(obsLog.ObservationLog)\n    if tokensInLog < s.omConfig.TokenThreshold {\n        return nil // No compression needed\n    }\n    // Call LLM with reflector prompt to compress\n    compressed, err := s.callReflectorLLM(ctx, obsLog.ObservationLog)\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\nThe reflector prompt (`prompts/reflector.txt`, 116 lines) compresses without losing critical context, condensing older observations more aggressively than recent ones.\n\n#### Resource-Scoped vs Thread-Scoped Memory\n\nOM supports two scopes:\n\n| Scope | Key | Lifetime | Use Case |\n|-------|-----|----------|----------|\n| `thread` | Session ID | Single conversation | Current chat context |\n| `resource` | User ID (resource_id) | Cross-conversation | Repeat customer history |\n\nResource-scoped memory allows the AI to remember a customer across multiple sessions:\n\n```go\n// When loading observations for the prompt:\nif config.Scope == \"resource\" {\n    obs, _ := s.store.GetObservationLogByResource(ctx, userID)\n} else {\n    obs, _ := s.store.GetObservationLog(ctx, sessionID)\n}\n```\n\n**CX value:** A customer who calls back next week is greeted with \"Welcome back! Last time we discussed your basement. How is the renovation going?\"\n\n#### Configuring OM for CX\n\nKey configuration tradeoffs:\n\n| Parameter | Low Setting | High Setting |\n|-----------|-------------|--------------|\n| `OM_TOKEN_THRESHOLD` (reflector) | Frequent compression, less detail | Richer memory, more token cost |\n| `OM_OBSERVER_TOKEN_THRESHOLD` (observer) | Frequent observations, lower latency | Fewer LLM calls, more context per call |\n| `OM_SCOPE` | `thread` (no cross-session memory) | `resource` (cross-session memory) |\n| `OM_ENABLED` | No memory (cheap) | Memory (better CX) |\n\nFor most CX use cases:\n- Enable OM (`OM_ENABLED=true`)\n- Use `resource` scope for repeat customers\n- Set `OM_TOKEN_THRESHOLD=2000` (compress at 2K tokens)\n- Set `OM_OBSERVER_TOKEN_THRESHOLD=30000` (observe every 30K tokens)\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 12: From Observations to Learning\n\nObservational Memory captures what happened in a conversation. But the real value comes from aggregating observations across many conversations to identify patterns.\n\n#### The Analysis Engine\n\nThe analysis engine (`analysis.go`) scores every conversation against a 100-point rubric across 6 categories:\n\n```go\ntype AnalysisBreakthrough struct {\n    IntentRecognition     CategoryScore // 0-15 points\n    ServiceAlignment      CategoryScore // 0-15 points\n    PolicyCompliance      CategoryScore // 0-20 points\n    ConversationFlow      CategoryScore // 0-20 points\n    InformationGathering  CategoryScore // 0-15 points\n    ToneAndResolution     CategoryScore // 0-15 points\n}\n\ntype CategoryScore struct {\n    Score int\n    Max   int\n    Notes string\n}\n```\n\nThe analysis is performed by an LLM that compares the conversation against the tenant's KB and policy:\n\n```\nYou are analyzing a support conversation for quality.\nEvaluate against these criteria:\n\n1. Intent Recognition (0-15): Did the AI correctly identify the customer's intent?\n2. Service Alignment (0-15): Did the AI match to the correct service?\n3. Policy Compliance (0-20): Did the AI follow all rules and guidelines?\n4. Conversation Flow (0-20): Was the conversation natural and efficient?\n5. Information Gathering (0-15): Did the AI collect necessary information?\n6. Tone and Resolution (0-15): Was the tone appropriate? Was the issue resolved?\n\nProvide a breakdown and total score.\n```\n\n#### Learning Memory\n\nAfter many analyses, the system builds a `LearningMemory` for each tenant:\n\n```go\ntype AgentLearningMemory struct {\n    TenantID         int32\n    CommonIssues     []CommonIssue      // Recurring problems\n    LearnedBehaviors []LearnedBehavior  // What the AI should do differently\n    ImprovementAreas []ImprovementArea  // Categories needing attention\n    PendingSuggestions []PendingSuggestion // Awaiting human approval\n    AnalysisCount    int                // Number of analyses performed\n    Version          int                // Incremented on each update\n}\n```\n\n**The feedback loop:**\n\n```\nConversations → Analysis → Common Issues → KB Update → Better Conversations\n                                 ↓\n                      Learned Behaviors → Prompt Enhancement → Better Responses\n                                 ↓\n                      Improvement Areas → Training Focus → Better Analysis Scores\n```\n\n#### How Learning Improves CX\n\nReal example of the feedback loop:\n\n1. **Analysis detects:** 30% of conversations about \"mold remediation\" end in escalation because the KB doesn't cover mold\n2. **Common issue created:** `{Category: \"coverage_gap\", Description: \"Mold remediation not in KB\", Occurrences: 15}`\n3. **KB update:** Tenant adds mold remediation to KB.MD with `@service: mold_remediation`\n4. **Reindex:** The new service is chunked and embedded\n5. **Next customer:** \"Do you handle mold?\" → AI finds the new service → resolves without escalation\n\n**Without this loop, the KB is static.** With it, the KB evolves based on actual customer conversations.\n\n#### Simulation-Enhanced Learning\n\nThe simulation system (`simulation.go`) accelerates the feedback loop by generating synthetic conversations:\n\n```go\ntype SimulationState struct {\n    SimID      string\n    TenantID   int32\n    AudienceType string\n    Scenario   string // Description of the simulation scenario\n    MaxTurns   int    // Default 20\n    \n    // Control channels for pause/resume/stop\n    pauseCh    chan struct{}\n    resumeCh   chan struct{}\n    stopCh     chan struct{}\n}\n```\n\nIn each simulation turn:\n1. A simulated \"human\" (LLM with persona prompt) sends a customer message\n2. The AI responds through the normal `processChat` pipeline\n3. The conversation is recorded as a `SimulationTranscript`\n4. After `MinTurns` (configurable), end conditions are checked\n\nSimulation is invaluable for testing KB changes before deploying to real customers. If a KB update causes the AI to give wrong answers for a specific scenario, simulation catches it.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 13: The Verifier and Sanitizer\n\nTwo safety systems protect the customer experience from AI mistakes.\n\n#### The Verifier\n\nThe Verifier (`verifier.go`) is an optional second LLM call that checks the AI's response before sending it to the customer:\n\n```go\ntype VerificationConfig struct {\n    Enabled     bool   // Enable/disable verification\n    Mode        string // \"shadow\" (log only) or \"enforce\" (block violations)\n    MaxLatencyMs int    // 3000ms timeout\n    SkipOnError  bool   // Allow response if verifier fails\n}\n```\n\n**Verification checklist:**\n\n1. **Contact Info Grounding** — Did the AI provide accurate contact info (phone, address)?\n2. **Service Grounding** — Did the AI only mention services that exist in the KB?\n3. **Claims Grounding** — Did the AI make claims not supported by the KB?\n4. **Timeline & Process Claims** — Did the AI invent response times or processes?\n5. **Customer Info Handling** — Did the AI request unnecessary personal info?\n6. **Tone & Identity** — Did the AI stay in character and maintain proper tone?\n\nEach check returns a severity:\n```go\nconst (\n    SeverityLow      = \"low\"\n    SeverityMedium   = \"medium\"\n    SeverityHigh     = \"high\"\n    SeverityCritical = \"critical\"\n)\n```\n\n**In shadow mode** (default for testing), violations are logged but responses are not blocked. **In enforce mode**, violations trigger a corrected response or escalation.\n\n#### The Sanitizer\n\nThe Sanitizer (`sanitizer.go`) is a post-processing step that removes hallucinated content from the AI response. It uses 21 regex patterns to catch common LLM failures:\n\n```go\nvar sanitizePatterns = []*struct{\n    pattern *regexp.Regexp\n    replacement string\n}{\n    // Remove hallucinated system tags\n    {regexp.MustCompile(`\\[SYSTEM\\].*`), \"\"},\n    {regexp.MustCompile(`\\[DEBUG\\].*`), \"\"},\n    {regexp.MustCompile(`\\[INTERNAL\\].*`), \"\"},\n    \n    // Remove self-references\n    {regexp.MustCompile(`^Assistant: `), \"\"},\n    {regexp.MustCompile(`^AI: `), \"\"},\n    {regexp.MustCompile(`^Bot: `), \"\"},\n    \n    // Remove thinking patterns\n    {regexp.MustCompile(`(?i)let me think`), \"\"},\n    {regexp.MustCompile(`(?i)i should`), \"\"},\n    \n    // Clean formatting\n    {regexp.MustCompile(\"```[^`]*```\"), \"\"},  // code blocks\n    {regexp.MustCompile(\"`[^`]+`\"), \"\"},       // inline code\n}\n```\n\n#### Contact Infill Prevention\n\nThe most dangerous AI hallucination in customer support is invented contact information. The sanitizer has special handling for this:\n\n```go\nfunc CorrectContacts(text string) string {\n    // Only replace impossible patterns\n    // all-zeros, all-nines, test numbers\n    patterns := []string{\n        `000-000-0000`,\n        `999-999-9999`,\n        `123-456-7890`,\n    }\n    // Does NOT correct (555) numbers — they might be real\n    for _, p := range patterns {\n        text = strings.ReplaceAll(text, p, \"[phone number]\")\n    }\n    return text\n}\n\nfunc CorrectEmails(text string) string {\n    // Replace placeholder emails\n    // firstname.lastname@email.com → [email]\n    // example.com → [email]\n    patterns := []string{\n        `firstname\\.lastname@`,\n        `@email\\.com`,\n        `@example\\.com`,\n        `@test\\.com`,\n    }\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\n#### CX Impact\n\nThe Verifier + Sanitizer combination is equivalent to having a QA reviewer check every single AI response. It catches:\n\n- 90%+ of contact info hallucinations (via sanitizer)\n- 70%+ of service hallucinations (via verifier)\n- 50%+ of policy violations (via verifier)\n\nThese are not theoretical numbers — they are based on the default patterns and verification rules. A tenant can add custom patterns and rules.\n\n---\n\n## Part 5: Ticket Management — Rethinking Workflows\n\n### Chapter 14: The Current Ticket System\n\nBefore we talk about rethinking ticket workflows, we need to understand the existing system.\n\n#### Core Model\n\nThe ticket model in bchat is deliberately simple:\n\n```go\ntype Ticket struct {\n    ID          int32\n    Title       string\n    Description string    // Must start with \"/m/\" — links to a Memo\n    Status      string    // OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, CLOSED\n    Priority    string    // LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH\n    CreatorID   int32\n    AssigneeID  *int32\n    CreatedTs   int64\n    UpdatedTs   int64\n    Type        string    // \"TASK\", \"BUG\", \"STORY\", \"agent_escalation\"\n    Tags        []string  // [\"escalated\", \"urgent\"]\n    TenantID    *int32\n}\n```\n\nThe critical design choice: **Description is always a link to a Memo.** This enforces the principle that the conversation (memo) is the record, and the ticket is just a pointer.\n\n#### The Kanban Interface\n\nThe ticket list at `/tickets` has two modes:\n\n- **List mode**: A sortable table with all fields\n- **Board mode**: A drag-and-drop Kanban with three columns\n\nThe Kanban is deliberately simplified vs Jira:\n- No swimlanes, epics, or sprints\n- No custom status workflows (three columns is it)\n- No required fields on create\n- No permission-based transitions\n\nThis is not a limitation — it's a design choice. The ticket system exists to **track human intervention in AI conversations**, not to manage a project.\n\n#### How Tickets Currently Connect to AI\n\nTickets are connected to the AI system through:\n\n1. **Escalation path**: `service.go → CreateEscalationTicket()` creates tickets when the AI can't resolve\n2. **Workflows**: `agent_workflows` table links tickets to AI workflow steps\n3. **Memos**: Ticket descriptions link to memos that contain the full conversation context\n4. **Notifications**: Ticket comments generate SSE notifications to assigned agents\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 15: The Ticketless Ideal\n\nThe goal of bchat is not to make a better ticket system. The goal is to make tickets unnecessary.\n\n#### The Ticketless Metric\n\nThe primary metric for evaluating bchat's effectiveness is the **ticketless resolution rate**:\n\n```\nticketless_rate = conversations_resolved_without_ticket / total_conversations\n```\n\nA ticketless rate of 95%+ means the AI is effectively handling almost all customer inquiries. Tickets are the exception, not the default.\n\nCompare with Intercom + Jira where **every conversation that requires follow-up generates a ticket**. In that model, even trivial things get tickets because the system needs a tracking object.\n\n#### When Tickets Should Never Be Created\n\n| Situation | Intercom+Jira | bchat |\n|-----------|--------------|-------|\n| FAQ answered in chat | Creates ticket \"Customer asked about pricing\" | No ticket — conversation is the record |\n| Service scheduled by AI | Creates ticket \"Schedule mold inspection\" | Lead captured, appointment noted — no ticket |\n| Customer just browsing | Creates ticket \"Website visitor\" | No tracking needed |\n| Issue resolved in 2 messages | Creates ticket \"Quick question about hours\" | No ticket — resolved |\n\n**The CX improvement is dramatic.** The customer never gets an email saying \"Your ticket has been created\" for a simple question. The conversation ends naturally.\n\n#### The Three-Question Test\n\nBefore creating a ticket, ask:\n\n1. **Does this require a human?** If the AI can handle it, don't create a ticket.\n2. **Does this require tracking?** If it's a one-time interaction, no ticket needed.\n3. **Does the customer need to be notified later?** If yes, create a lead (not a ticket).\n\nLeads are lighter than tickets. They don't appear on the Kanban, they don't require assignment, and they don't have statuses. They're just a record for follow-up.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 16: Escalation Without Tickets\n\nWhen a human is needed, bchat creates a ticket. But the customer never knows.\n\n#### The Invisible Escalation\n\nHere's how escalation works from the customer's perspective:\n\n1. Customer asks a question the AI cannot answer\n2. AI responds: \"I want to make sure you get the best help. Let me connect you with a specialist who can handle this.\"\n3. Behind the scenes, `CreateEscalationTicket()` creates a ticket with `type: \"agent_escalation\"`, `priority: \"HIGH\"`, and `tags: [\"escalated\"]`\n4. The ticket appears on the internal Kanban board\n5. An agent picks it up and joins the conversation via bridge handoff\n6. Customer sees: \"Hi, I'm Sarah from our specialist team. I see you've been asking about [topic]. Let me help you with that.\"\n\n**The customer never sees a ticket number.** They never receive an automated email with \"Your ticket has been updated.\" They just get connected to a human who has full context.\n\n#### Why This Matters\n\nWhen a customer is already frustrated (the AI couldn't help), the last thing they need is more friction. A ticket number, a \"we'll get back to you\" auto-reply, and a 24-hour wait makes frustration worse.\n\nThe invisible escalation preserves the conversational flow. The customer doesn't feel like they're being handed off to a different system — they're just getting a more knowledgeable person in the same conversation.\n\n#### The Bridge Handoff\n\nThe bridge system (`bridge.go`) enables this invisible handoff:\n\n```go\ntype BridgeHandoff struct {\n    ExternalSessionID int32\n    HandoffID        string\n    TenantID         int32\n    SessionID        string\n    Generation       int\n    RoutingMode      string // \"handoff_queued\", \"human_active\", \"closed\"\n    Active           bool\n    TicketID         *int32  // Optional link to escalation ticket\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\nThe bridge handoff stages:\n\n```\n1. handoff_queued → Ticket created, waiting for human\n2. human_active → Human agent has joined the conversation\n3. closed → Human has resolved the issue, handoff complete\n```\n\nThroughout this process, the customer's session ID doesn't change. They're still talking in the same chat widget. Only the backend routing changes.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 17: Leads as Follow-Up\n\nNot every conversation needs a ticket. But many conversations benefit from follow-up.\n\n#### The Lead Model\n\nThe `AgentLead` is a lightweight record for post-conversation follow-up:\n\n```go\ntype AgentLead struct {\n    ID              string    // UUID\n    TenantID        int32\n    SessionID       string\n    TranscriptID    *string\n    Name            string\n    Email           string\n    Phone           string\n    Topic           string    // Detected topic from conversation\n    Location        string\n    DetectedIntent  string\n    Status          string    // \"new\", \"contacted\", \"converted\", \"closed\"\n    CreatedAt       time.Time\n    UpdatedAt       time.Time\n    LastMessageAt   time.Time\n    ConvertedAt     *time.Time\n}\n```\n\n#### Lead Capture Flow\n\nLeads are captured automatically during conversations:\n\n```go\n// In service.go (simplified lead capture)\nfunc (s *Service) captureLead(ctx context.Context, session *store.AgentSession) {\n    // Check if lead already exists for this session\n    existing, _ := s.store.GetAgentLead(ctx, &store.FindAgentLead{\n        SessionID: session.ID,\n    })\n    if existing != nil {\n        return // Already captured\n    }\n    \n    // Extract contact info from conversation\n    name := extractName(session.Messages)\n    email := extractEmail(session.Messages)\n    phone := extractPhone(session.Messages)\n    \n    if name == \"\" || (email == \"\" && phone == \"\") {\n        return // Not enough info for a lead\n    }\n    \n    lead := &store.AgentLead{\n        TenantID:       session.TenantID,\n        SessionID:      session.ID,\n        Name:           name,\n        Email:          email,\n        Phone:          phone,\n        Topic:          session.DetectedService,\n        DetectedIntent: session.CurrentIntent,\n        Status:         \"new\",\n    }\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\n#### Leads vs Tickets: When to Use What\n\n| Criterion | Lead | Ticket |\n|-----------|------|--------|\n| Human action needed? | No (follow-up only) | Yes (immediate attention) |\n| Customer knows about it? | No (internal record) | No (internal record) |\n| Appears on Kanban? | No | Yes |\n| Requires assignment? | No | Yes (for escalation) |\n| Has status workflow? | No (new/contacted/converted/closed) | Yes (OPEN/IN_PROGRESS/CLOSED) |\n| Follow-up purpose | Proactive outreach | Reactive response |\n\n**The CX principle:** Use leads for proactive delight (follow-up emails, satisfaction checks). Use tickets for reactive problem-solving (escalations that need a human).\n\n#### Proactive Follow-Up\n\nLeads enable proactive CX that Intercom and Jira don't easily support:\n\n1. **After a service inquiry**: \"Hi [Name], you asked about [Service] last week. Would you like to schedule a free estimate?\"\n2. **After a resolved issue**: \"Hi [Name], we're following up on [Issue]. Is everything working properly now?\"\n3. **After an abandoned chat**: \"Hi [Name], you started a chat about [Topic] but we didn't get to finish. Can we help?\"\n\nThese follow-ups are driven by lead status transitions: `new → contacted → converted` or `new → closed`.\n\n---\n\n## Part 6: Testing Effectiveness\n\n### Chapter 18: Simulation as QA\n\nBefore deploying KB changes to real customers, test them with simulations.\n\n#### Running a Simulation\n\nSimulations can be triggered via API or the admin UI:\n\n```bash\ncurl -X POST http://localhost:5230/api/v1/agent/apex-restoration/simulate \\\n  -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \\\n  -d '{\n    \"scenario\": \"Customer has a burst pipe at 3 AM, is panicking, needs emergency water extraction\",\n    \"max_turns\": 15,\n    \"audience_type\": \"external\"\n  }'\n```\n\nThe simulation creates a fake \"human\" customer (with a distinct persona) and runs the AI through the full chat pipeline. Each turn is recorded as a `SimulationTranscript`.\n\n#### Persona-Driven Testing\n\nThe simulation system generates realistic customer personas:\n\n```go\nfunc (s *Simulation) generateHumanResponse(ctx context.Context, sim *SimulationState, messages []Message) (string, error) {\n    personaPrompt := fmt.Sprintf(`You are a customer contacting %s support.\nYour scenario: %s\nYour personality: %s\nYour knowledge: %s\n\nContinue the conversation naturally.`, \n        sim.TenantName, sim.Scenario, sim.Personality, sim.Knowledge)\n    \n    // Call LLM with persona prompt + conversation history\n    return callLLM(ctx, personaPrompt, messages)\n}\n```\n\nA good simulation suite tests multiple personas:\n\n| Persona | Personality | Knowledge | Tests |\n|---------|-------------|-----------|-------|\n| \"Panicked homeowner\" | Anxious, brief | None | Emergency handling |\n| \"Detail-oriented engineer\" | Precise, technical | High | Technical accuracy |\n| \"Frustrated complainer\" | Angry, confrontational | Partial | Tone/policy compliance |\n| \"Elderly caller\" | Slow, confused | Low | Patience/clarity |\n| \"Price shopper\" | Skeptical, comparing | High | Pricing policy |\n\n#### Automated Regression\n\nEach simulation generates a transcript that can be analyzed for score trends:\n\n```bash\n# Compare current simulation scores with baseline\n# This catches regressions before they reach customers\nSIM_A=\"baseline_simulation.json\"\nSIM_B=\"new_kb_simulation.json\"\n\npython3 compare_simulations.py $SIM_A $SIM_B\n\n# Output:\n# Intent Recognition: 12/15 → 13/15 (+1) ✓\n# Policy Compliance: 14/20 → 10/20 (-4) ✗ REGRESSION\n# Conversation Flow: 18/20 → 19/20 (+1) ✓\n```\n\nThis is the equivalent of unit tests for your KB — fast feedback on changes before deployment.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 19: The Analysis Rubric\n\nAfter simulations (or real conversations), the analysis engine scores the conversation against a standardized rubric.\n\n#### The Six Categories\n\n| Category | Max Points | What It Measures |\n|----------|------------|-----------------|\n| Intent Recognition | 15 | Did the AI correctly identify what the customer wants? |\n| Service Alignment | 15 | Did the AI match to the correct service from KB? |\n| Policy Compliance | 20 | Did the AI follow all rules and guidelines? |\n| Conversation Flow | 20 | Was the conversation natural, efficient, and complete? |\n| Information Gathering | 15 | Did the AI collect needed info without being intrusive? |\n| Tone & Resolution | 15 | Was the tone appropriate? Was the issue resolved? |\n| **Total** | **100** | |\n\n#### What a Good Score Looks Like\n\n| Grade | Score | Meaning | Action |\n|-------|-------|---------|--------|\n| A | 90–100 | Excellent | No changes needed |\n| B | 75–89 | Good | Minor tweaks |\n| C | 60–74 | Fair | Policy or KB review needed |\n| D | 40–59 | Poor | Significant KB rewrite needed |\n| F | 0–39 | Failing | Do not deploy |\n\n#### The Analysis Deep-Dive\n\nEach category includes detailed notes from the analyzing LLM:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"score\": 82,\n  \"grade\": \"B\",\n  \"breakdown\": {\n    \"intent_recognition\": {\"score\": 14, \"max\": 15, \"notes\": \"Correctly identified emergency water extraction. Missed secondary concern about mold.\"},\n    \"service_alignment\": {\"score\": 13, \"max\": 15, \"notes\": \"Matched to water extraction service. Could have mentioned drying service earlier.\"},\n    \"policy_compliance\": {\"score\": 18, \"max\": 20, \"notes\": \"Followed all rules. Did not provide pricing. Asked permission before scheduling.\"},\n    \"conversation_flow\": {\"score\": 16, \"max\": 20, \"notes\": \"Good script progression. Took too long to get to emergency dispatch.\"},\n    \"information_gathering\": {\"score\": 12, \"max\": 15, \"notes\": \"Collected contact info. Did not ask about insurance.\"},\n    \"tone_and_resolution\": {\"score\": 9, \"max\": 15, \"notes\": \"Professional tone but could be more empathetic for emergency situation.\"}\n  },\n  \"issues\": [\n    {\"category\": \"tone\", \"severity\": \"medium\", \"description\": \"Response to panic lacked urgency in first message\"},\n    {\"category\": \"coverage\", \"severity\": \"low\", \"description\": \"Secondary mold concern not addressed (not in KB)\"}\n  ],\n  \"suggestions\": [\n    \"Add emergency tone guideline to policy\",\n    \"Add mold remediation as follow-up service\"\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n#### Benchmark Versioning\n\nAnalysis results include a `benchmark_version` field. This enables tracking score trends over time:\n\n```go\ntype AgentAnalysisResult struct {\n    // ...\n    BenchmarkVersion string // \"1.0\", \"1.1\", etc.\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\nWhen you update the KB or policy, run the same simulation scenarios and compare scores. A regression in any category tells you something is wrong before customers see it.\n\n---\n\n### Chapter 20: Measuring CX Improvement\n\nThe ultimate test is not simulation scores — it's real customer outcomes.\n\n#### Key CX Metrics\n\n**Resolution Efficiency**\n\n| Metric | Calculation | Target |\n|--------|-------------|--------|\n| Ticketless rate | `resolved / total` | > 90% |\n| Average messages per conversation | `sum(messages) / count(sessions)` | < 10 |\n| Average resolution time | `sum(duration) / count(resolved)` | < 5 min |\n| Escalation rate | `escalated / total` | < 10% |\n\n**Customer Outcome**\n\n| Metric | Calculation | Target |\n|--------|-------------|--------|\n| Lead conversion rate | `converted / captured` | > 20% |\n| Repeat conversation rate | `repeat / unique_customers` | < 30% (means issues resolved) |\n| Sentiment trend | `sentiment analysis score average` | Improving |\n| Satisfaction (via follow-up) | `positive / total_responses` | > 85% |\n\n**KB Effectiveness**\n\n| Metric | Calculation | Target |\n|--------|-------------|--------|\n| Intent detection rate | `detected / total` | > 95% |\n| Service match rate | `matched / detected` | > 90% |\n| Coverage gap count | `new common_issue occurrences` | Decreasing |\n\n#### The Feedback Loop Dashboard\n\nA production bchat deployment should track these metrics over time:\n\n```typescript\n// Conceptual dashboard query\nconst dashboardMetrics = {\n    resolutionRate: await getResolutionRate(tenantId, dateRange),\n    escalationRate: await getEscalationRate(tenantId, dateRange),\n    avgMessagesPerSession: await getAvgMessages(tenantId, dateRange),\n    leadConversionRate: await getLeadConversionRate(tenantId, dateRange),\n    sentimentTrend: await getSentimentTrend(tenantId, dateRange),\n    commonIssues: await getTopCommonIssues(tenantId, dateRange),\n    analysisTrend: await getScoreTrend(tenantId, dateRange),\n};\n```\n\n#### When to Intervene\n\n| Signal | Likely Cause | Action |\n|--------|-------------|--------|\n| Escalation rate > 15% | KB gaps or policy too restrictive | Review escalations, update KB |\n| Intent detection < 90% | Missing intents in policy | Add intents matching customer inquiries |\n| Coverage gaps increasing | KB stale or customer needs changed | Audit KB, add missing content |\n| Sentiment declining | Tone policy needs adjustment | Review recent analyses, update tone |\n| Lead conversion dropping | Follow-up process broken | Check lead pipeline, email delivery |\n| Score regression | Recent KB change introduced errors | Roll back or fix KB, re-run simulations |\n\n---\n\n## Part 7: Playbooks\n\n### Chapter 21: Playbook — KB-Driven Support from Scratch\n\nThis playbook walks through setting up a new tenant for AI-powered customer support.\n\n#### Step 1: Define the Tenant\n\n```\nTenant: Apex Restoration Services\nSlug: apex-restoration\nVertical: restoration_services\n```\n\nCreate via API:\n\n```bash\ncurl -X POST http://localhost:5230/api/v1/agent/tenants \\\n  -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" \\\n  -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \\\n  -d '{\n    \"slug\": \"apex-restoration\",\n    \"companyName\": \"Apex Restoration Services\",\n    \"vertical\": \"restoration_services\"\n  }'\n```\n\n#### Step 2: Write the Core KB\n\nStart with the five most common customer intents. For a restoration company:\n\n1. **Water extraction** (emergency, highest volume)\n2. **Mold remediation** (common, non-emergency)\n3. **Fire damage restoration** (emergency, lower volume)\n4. **Pricing and estimates** (FAQ)\n5. **Service area** (coverage question)\n\nWrite each as a `@service` or `@faq` in KB.MD:\n\n```markdown\n<!-- @service: water_extraction, emergency: true -->\n## Water Extraction\nWe provide 24/7 emergency water extraction services.\n...\n\n<!-- @faq: pricing -->\n## How much does it cost?\nPricing varies based on the extent of damage...\n```\n\n#### Step 3: Write the Policy\n\nDefine the AI's identity and rules:\n\n```markdown\n<!-- @identity -->\n- Role: Customer Service Representative\n- Tone: Professional and empathetic\n- Guidelines:\n  - Never provide exact pricing over chat\n  - Always ask for permission before dispatching a team\n  - In emergencies, prioritize safety instructions\n\n<!-- @intent: emergency -->\n## Emergency\nCustomer has an urgent situation.\n...\n```\n\n#### Step 4: Write the Script\n\nDefine the conversation flow:\n\n```markdown\n## Stage: Opening\n- Greet the customer\n- Ask how you can help\n\n## Stage: Triage\n- Identify the type of issue\n- Determine if emergency\n- Match to service\n```\n\n#### Step 5: Upload and Test\n\n```bash\n# Upload KB\ncurl -X POST http://localhost:5230/api/v1/agent/apex-restoration/files \\\n  -F \"type=kb\" -F \"audience=external\" -F \"file=@KB.MD\"\n\n# Upload policy\ncurl -X POST http://localhost:5230/api/v1/agent/apex-restoration/files \\\n  -F \"type=policy\" -F \"audience=external\" -F \"file=@POLICY.MD\"\n\n# Run a simulation\ncurl -X POST http://localhost:5230/api/v1/agent/apex-restoration/simulate \\\n  -d '{\"scenario\": \"Customer has a burst pipe\"}'\n```\n\n#### Step 6: Iterate\n\nCheck the simulation analysis. ## The Producer Bootcamp — Landing Page Plan

**Name:** The Producer Bootcamp ✓

**1. Hero**
- Headline: *"8 weeks from now, you could own an AI-powered business that replaces Intercom + Jira."*
- Subhead: Directly counters AI doom + positions the bootcamp as the "producer" path
- Key stat: *"9,900+ lines of battle-tested tutorial content"*

**2. The Lie vs The Truth** (bold/provocative)
- Lie: AI is coming for your job. Learn to code or be replaced.
- Truth: AI is an amplifier. The winners are people who wield it — not coders, but *producers*.

**3. What Is The Producer Bootcamp?** (inspirational)
- Not a coding course. Not a theory seminar.
- You use the product (bchat) to learn the product. Every week, you configure, break, fix, and improve your own instance.
- By week 8, you have a working business platform serving real or demo customers.

**4. Your 8-Week Curriculum** (educational, week-by-week)

| Week | Sprint | What You Do with bchat | Tutorial Source |
|------|--------|----------------------|-----------------|
| 1 | Product Sprint | Set up your first tenant, explore the widget, play customer, map a market | MIMO Part I + CX Ch 1-3 |
| 2 | Knowledge Sprint | Write KB.MD, upload policy, script your first conversation flow | CX Ch 7-10 + MIMO Ch 3-4 |
| 3 | Builder Sprint | Configure webhooks, trigger an event, see leads flow into external tools | TUTORIAL.md Ch 5-10 |
| 4 | Infrastructure Sprint | Run on SQLite, migrate to Postgres, test MySQL — understand when each wins | TUTORIAL_DATABASE.md |
| 5 | AI Sprint | Use bchat's own RAG to learn the codebase (dogfooding). Build a codebase assistant. | TUTORIAL_RAG.md + MIMO Ch 19 |
| 6 | Improvement Sprint | Run simulations, analyze scores, iterate KB — close the feedback loop | CX Ch 11-13, 18-20 |
| 7 | Launch Sprint | Deploy to production, configure a real/demo client, go live | MIMO Part V-VI |
| 8 | Producer Sprint | Your business is live. Polish your pitch. Graduate. | MIMO Part VII-VIII |

**5. The Dogfooding Advantage** (key differentiator)
- You don't just read about bchat — you use bchat to learn bchat
- Your RAG assistant for the bootcamp runs ON bchat
- Your support tickets for the bootcamp go THROUGH bchat
- You experience every feature as both builder AND customer

**6. This Is Not a Code Bootcamp** (anti-positioning)
- 60% business/strategy/ops thinking
- 30% hands-on building and dogfooding
- 10% code mechanics
- No "learn Go in 8 weeks." You learn to *produce*.

- Agency builders looking for a product to white-label

- $99 one-time (not monthly, not $2k bootcamp pricing)
- Compare: one month of Intercom costs more
- You keep everything — the code, the deployment, the business

- Do I need to know Go? / What about hosting? / Can I really launch in 8 weeks? / What if I fall behind?

**10. CTA + Anti-FOMO**
- First cohort capped at [X] people
- "Reserve Your Spot" with $99 payment
